Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 1–8:

(p-77) In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah Ta-Ha

This surah is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and thirty-five.

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Ta-Ha.﴾ ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder to whoever fears [God].﴾ ﴿A revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Compassionate, who is established upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿God—there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾

People have differed regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾, in accordance with their differing about all the letters mentioned at the beginnings of surahs, except the view of one who said that the letters here are a reference to the letters of the alphabet, as one says "alif, ba, jim," for this does not apply here, since what follows "Ta-Ha" in speech cannot validly be a predicate of "Ta-Ha."

"Ta-Ha" has been specified with opinions that do not apply to the beginnings of the surahs mentioned. Among them is the view of one who said: "Ta-Ha" is one of the names of Muhammad (ﷺ). Another said: "Ta-Ha" means "O man" in Syriac, and it was said: in another of the non-Arabic languages. It is also reported that it is a Yemeni dialect of 'Akk, and al-Tabari recited in this regard:

؎ I called Ta-Ha in the battle, but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be turning aside from it.

(p-78) It is also narrated: "muzayilan" (departing). Another said:

؎ Indeed, foolishness, Ta-Ha, is among your traits; may God not bless the cursed people.

A group said: the cause of the revelation of the verse is only that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) bore the hardship of prayer, such that his feet would swell and he needed rest. So it was said to him: "Ta" the earth, meaning: do not exert yourself until you need rest. Thus the pronoun in "Ta-Ha" refers to the earth, and the hamza was lightened so that it became a quiescent alif.

A group read "Ta-Ha," and its origin is "Ta'," so the hamza was dropped and the silent ha' (ha' al-sakt) was added. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "Ta-Ha" with fatha on the ta' and the ha', and this is related from Qalun from Nafi'. Ya'qub narrated from him kasra, and it is also related from him as between fatha and kasra. Some read with imala, and others with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation), and tafkhim is the dialect of the Hijaz and of the Prophet (ﷺ). 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Ta-Ha" with kasra on the ta' and the ha'. Abu 'Amr read "Ta-Ha" with fatha on the ta' and kasra on the ha'. It is related from al-Dahhak and 'Amr ibn Fa'id that they both recited: "Ta-wi."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: "li-tashqa" (to make you distressed), its meaning is to exert yourself beyond your capacity in worship and standing in prayer. A group said: the cause of the verse is that the Quraysh looked at the livelihood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his austerity and the abundance of his dependents, and said: "Muhammad is in misery with his Lord." So the verse was revealed rejecting them, meaning: God, Exalted is He, did not send down the Qur'an to make Muhammad miserable, but to make him the happiest of the children of Adam in everlasting bliss at the highest ranks. The misery you saw is the comfort of the soul, and there is no misery with that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

(p-79) This interpretation is more general than the first regarding the word "shaqa" (misery).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿but as a reminder to whoever fears [God]﴾ may be in the accusative as a substitute for the position of ﴿to make you distressed﴾, and it may be in the accusative by a hidden verb whose estimate is: "but We sent it down as a reminder." "Yakhsha" (fears) includes faith and righteous deeds, since fear is what motivates these. His saying: ﴿A revelation﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and His saying: ﴿from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ is a qualifier which he placed in the position of the qualified, and this conveys admonition, reminder, belittling of idols, and stirring of souls to reflection. "Al-'ula" is the plural of "'ulya," on the pattern fu'la.

His saying: ﴿The Compassionate﴾ is in the nominative as a subject, and it may be a substitute for the pronoun in "khalaqa" (created). His saying: ﴿is established﴾ — a group said: it means "took possession" (istawla). Abu al-Ma'ali and others among the theologians said: it means the establishment of domination and supremacy. Sufyan al-Thawri said: He did an act upon the Throne and named it "istiwa'." Al-Sha'bi and a group besides him said: this is among the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an; we believe in it and do not pursue its meaning. Malik ibn Anas was asked by a man about this "istiwa'," and Malik said to him: "The establishment is known, the modality is unknown, and asking about this is an innovation; I think you are an evil man. Remove him from me." The questioner turned away, saying: "O Abu 'Abd Allah, I asked about it the people of Syria and the people of Iraq, and none of them was granted success in it as you were."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Abu al-Ma'ali weakened the view of one who said: it is not to be spoken about in its interpretation. For if he says that every believer agrees that the word "istiwa'" is not in its customary sense in the usage of the Mighty Book, then when he does this, he has necessarily interpreted, and there is no benefit in delaying the seeking of the correct meaning and a clear way out. Rather, that causes confusion among people and misleads the common folk. The discussion of the matter of "istiwa'" has already preceded.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a continuation of the aforementioned attribute, alerting to the Creator, the Bestower of blessings. In His saying: ﴿and whatever is beneath the soil﴾ there is a narrative about the matter of the fish and the like, which I have abridged because of its lack of authenticity. The verse implies that every existent created thing belongs to God by ownership and origination, and there is no eternal being other than Him, Exalted is He. "Al-tara" means moist earth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you speak aloud﴾ — the verse — its meaning: and if you, O people, when you wish to inform someone of a matter, or to address your idols and others, speak aloud, (p-80) then indeed God, whose attributes are these, knows the secret and what is more hidden. The address with "ta-jhar" is to Muhammad (ﷺ), but what is meant by it is all people, since it is a verse of admonition.

People have differed about the ordering of "the secret" and what is more hidden than it. A group said: the secret is the quiet, faint speech, like reciting silently in prayer, and "what is more hidden" is what is within the soul as something settled. Another group said: the secret is what is in the souls of human beings and everything that can be in them in the future according to what is possible among human knowledge, and "what is more hidden" is what is among the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, which human beings can never know at all.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this is known to God, Mighty and Majestic. It has been interpreted on the authority of some of the early generation (salaf) that they made "wa-akhfa" (and more hidden) a past-tense verb, but this is weak.

By "the most beautiful names" he means the named realities which contain meanings that are at the utmost of goodness, and he used the singular adjective with the plural of the described because the named things do not have intellect, and this runs in the manner of ﴿other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha 18] and ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba' 10], and others. The scholars have mentioned that these are the names concerning which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: «Indeed God has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever counts them enters Paradise.»

(p-77) In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

This surah is Meccan, and its verses number one hundred and thirty-five.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

(p-79) This interpretation is more general than the first regarding the word "shaqa" (misery).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 9–14:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I may bring you a burning brand from it, or find guidance at the fire."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses! Indeed I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.﴾ ﴿Indeed I am God; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾

This interrogative is a *tawqif* (a prompt to attention), whose implication is to alert the soul to what is about to be presented to it. This is like when you begin speaking to a man because you want to inform him of a strange matter, so you say, "Did you know such-and-such?" and then you go on to tell him. The element governing *idh* ("when") is what is contained in His, glorified be He, words: ﴿the story of Moses﴾, which carries the sense of a verb. Its implied form is: "Has there reached you what Moses did when he saw a fire," and the like.

Now, among the account of Moses, peace be upon him, is that he departed from Madyan with his family, the daughter of Shu'ayb, intending the land of Egypt. The duration of his offence there had been long, so he hoped that his affair would remain hidden. He was, as they claim, a man of jealousy, so he would travel by night with his family and not travel by day, out of fear of the people discovering them. He lost his way on a dark, damp night. It is also related that he ran out of water and did not know where to seek it. While he was in this state, having struck his flint without producing any spark, he saw a fire. He said to his family, "Stay," meaning, "Remain." He went to the fire and found it blazing in a green, flourishing tree. It was said that the tree was a jujube tree (*unnab*), and it was said it was a thornbush (*awsaj*), and it was said it was a dodder (*'ulayqa*). When he approached it, it moved away from him and went on; when he turned back from it, it followed him. When he saw this, he became certain that this was a matter of God, exalted be He, that breaks customary habit. He was called, and his affair was settled on that night. This is the view of the majority, and it is the truth. Al-Naqqash related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he remained in that matter for a year, and his family stayed. They said: this is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is weak in itself.

*Anastu* means "I perceived." From it is the verse of al-Harith ibn Hilliza:

"She perceived a sound, and the spear-tips frightened her in the afternoon, when evening had drawn near."

A fire at a distance is perceived only by sight, and for this reason some of them explained the word as "I saw." *Anasa* is more general than *ra'a*, because you say, "I perceived from so-and-so good or evil."

*Al-qabas* is an ember of fire on the tip of a stick, or a reed, or the like. *Al-huda* here means the path, i.e., "Perhaps I will find someone guiding me or a guide, even if it is not a path." *Al-huda* encompasses all of this, and Moses, peace be upon him, only hoped for guidance regarding his situation, but he encountered guidance in its absolute sense.

In the mention of the entire story of Moses, peace be upon him, in this surah, there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning what he met with in conveying the message of hardships and the disbelief of the people. It is for him by way of example regarding his own affair. It is related from Nafi' and Hamza, "*fa-qala li-ahlihi imkuthu*" with a *damma* on the *ha'*, and likewise in *al-Qasas*; the rest read with a *kasra* on the *ha'* in both.

As for His, exalted be He, words: ﴿When he came to it﴾, the pronoun refers to the fire. His words ﴿he was called﴾ are a metaphor for God's speaking to him. In "*nuddiya*" there is a pronoun that stands in place of the subject, though if you wish you may make it Moses, since his mention has already occurred. Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *"inni"* (with a *kasra* on the alif) as a fresh beginning. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *"anni"* (with a *fatha* on the alif), meaning: "because I am your Lord, so take off your sandals." *Nuddiya* may be followed by a preposition, and Abu 'Ali recited:

"I called by the name of Rabi'a ibn Mukaddam, indeed the one whose name is renowned, trusted."

The commentators differed about the reason for which he was commanded to take off his sandals. One group said: they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so he was commanded to cast off the impurity. Another group said: rather, his sandals were of the hide of a slaughtered cow, but he was commanded to take them off so that he might receive the blessing of the sacred valley and so that his feet might touch the soil of the valley.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The verse may bear another meaning, which in my view is the most fitting: God commanded him to humble himself before the great state in which he found himself. The custom among kings is that sandals are removed, and a person reaches the utmost of humility. So Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to do this in this manner, and it does not matter whether his sandals were of carrion or otherwise.

*Al-muqaddas* means "the purified." *Tuwa* means "twice twice." One group said its meaning is: "Sanctify twice." Another group said its meaning is: "You folded it (*tawaytahu*)," i.e., you traversed it, meaning the land was folded for you twice, from your thought. Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *"Tuwan"* with tanwin, as the name of the place; Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read *"Tuwa"* without tanwin, as the name of the locality. All of these read with a *damma* on the *ta'*. Abu Zayd, from Abu 'Amr, read with a *kasra* on the *ta'*. A group read *"Tawi"*, and a group said it is the name of the valley. *Tuwa*, according to the first interpretation, is like their saying *thunan wa thunan*, meaning "repeatedly."

The seven readers other than Hamza read: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾. This recitation is supported by its harmony with His words ﴿I am your Lord﴾. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: *"wa-inni ikhtartuka"*. Hamza alone read: *"wa-inna ikhtarnaka"* with the plural and a *fatha* on the hamza with a shadda on the *nun*. The verse, according to this reading, is like His words: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra' 17:1], then He said: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Isra' 17:2], moving from singular to plural. A group read *"wa-inna ikhtarnaka"* with a *kasra* on the alif. My father, may God have mercy on him, related to me, saying: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say: When it was said to Moses, peace be upon him, "Listen to what is revealed," he stood upon a stone, leaned against a stone, placed his right hand upon his left, laid his chin upon his chest, and stood listening. All his clothing was wool. A group read: *"bil-wadi al-muqaddasi tawi"*.

His, exalted be He, words: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ may mean: "for My being remembered in it," or it may mean: "so that I may remember you in the highest place (*'illiyyin*) by means of it." On this view, the verbal noun may be construed as genitive of the agent or of the object, and the *lam* is the *lam* of cause. Another group said: His words "*li-dhikri*" mean "at the time of My remembrance," i.e., when you remember Me, and My command to you to do it. On this view, the *lam* has the same function as in His words: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra' 17:78]. A group read *"lil-dhikra"*, a group read *"li-dhikra"* without definiteness, and a group read *"lil-dhikr"*.

Another group said: its meaning is "I almost conceal it from Myself," as an expression of the intensity of its obscurity to created beings. Another group said: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost—" and the sentence is complete there, meaning: "I almost carry it out, because of its nearness and the certainty of its occurrence," and then He resumed the report that He conceals it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an unsettled opinion.

Another group said: "akādu" is superfluous and has no bearing on the meaning; rather the verse conveys the report that the Hour is coming, and that God conceals the time of its arrival from people.

(p-86) Another group said: "akādu" means "I want," so the meaning is: "I want to conceal it from you, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for." The proponent of this view cited the poet's line:

This meaning has already been mentioned.

Another group said: "akādu" retains its basic meaning, that of approaching what has not yet occurred. But the speech follows the Arabs' figurative usage and metaphor. Since the verse expresses the intensity of the concealment of the matter and the time of the Resurrection, and since certainty of its coming together with ignorance of its time is more awe-inspiring to souls, the Exalted's saying exaggerates in obscuring its time, saying: "I almost conceal it," to the point that it would not appear at all. But that does not happen, and it must appear.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a summary of this meaning, to which some of the exegetes pointed, and it is the strongest in my view. Some of those who held that the meaning is "I almost conceal it from Myself" transmitted what is unsettled in that saying, and so they said: the meaning of "from Myself" is: from My own accord and from My own side.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a rejection of the first meaning and a return to the view we chose last. So reflect on it.

The "lām" in the Exalted's saying "li-tujzā" (so that it may be recompensed) is connected to "āti'a" (coming), and so the threat is arranged in this order. "Tasʿā" means: it earns and commits.

The pronoun in His saying, "fa-lā yaṣuddannaka ʿanhā" (so let not divert you from it), refers to "the Hour," meaning belief in the Hour. He used the pronoun for it. It may also refer to the prayer. Another group said it refers to "there is no god but God."

(p-87) The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a likely reading, but the first two are clearer in meaning.

The Exalted's saying "fa-tardā" means: you will perish. "Al-radā" is destruction. From it is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

They called out, saying: "The horses have caused a horseman to perish!"
I said: "Is it the worship of God, that destruction of yours?"

This entire address is to Moses, peace be upon him, and so is what follows. Al-Naqqash said: the address in "fa-lā yaṣuddannaka ʿanhā" is to Muhammad (ﷺ). This is far-fetched. In the codex of ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, it reads: "akādu ukhfīhā min nafsī" (I almost conceal it from Myself), and on this reading the earlier opinion is built.

The Exalted's saying, "wa-mā tilka bi-yamīnika yā Mūsā" (And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?), its implied meaning is to alert and to gather the self to receive what is presented to it. Otherwise, God, Exalted is He, already knows what it is from eternity. His saying "bi-yamīnika" is attached to "tilka" (that). This is like the poet's saying:

"ʿAdas! What authority does ʿAbbad have over you?
You escaped, and this one you carry is a captive."

Ibn al-Jawhari said: It is reported in some traditions that God, Exalted is He, rebuked Moses for attributing the staff to himself on that occasion. He was told: "Throw it down," so that he might see its wonder, and know that he has no ownership over it and that it does not belong to him.

(p-88) Al-Hasan and Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read "ʿaṣāyī" with a kasrah on the yā' like "ghulāmī." A group read "ʿaṣā," which is the dialect of Hudhayl. From it is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

They outpaced my passion and gave their own desires free rein.

The majority read "ʿaṣāya" with a fatḥah on the yā'. Ibn Abi Ishaq likewise read "ʿaṣāy" with a sukūn on the yā'.

Then Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned from the benefits of his staff its greatest and most significant ones, and summarized the rest. The majority read "wa-ahushshu" with a dammah on the hā' and a dotted shīn, meaning: I strike the tree with it so that its leaves fall for the sheep. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "wa-ahishshu" with a kasrah on the hā', and the meaning is as stated before. ʿIkrimah, the client of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with both of them, read "wa-ahussu" with a dammah on the hā' and an undotted sīn, meaning: I drive them off and frighten them. Some read "ʿalā ghanamī" with a kasrah (genitive), and some read "ʿalā ghanamī" (taking the verb as governing the sheep). (p-89) Some read "ghanmī" with a sukūn on the nūn, and I do not know a basis for it. As for His saying "ukhrā" (other), He used the singular feminine form even though the preceding noun was plural. This is the common usage for the followers of plurals of non-rational things and their pronouns, since these are treated as if they were a single feminine noun, as in His saying: "al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā" (the most beautiful names) [Ṭā-Hā 8], and His saying: "yā jibālu awwibī maʿahu" (O mountains, echo with him) [Saba' 10]. The discussion of this point has already passed more than once.

The staff of Moses, peace be upon him, is the one he had taken from the house of the staves of the prophets, which was with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, when they agreed upon the flock. The staff of Adam, peace be upon him, was what he descended with from Paradise, and it was from the ʿayn-wood in the leaf of basil, meaning the elongated body in its middle. The explanation of its matter has already been mentioned earlier.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 19–35:**

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Moses."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said, "Seize it and do not fear. We will return it to its original form."﴾ ﴿"And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white, without harm, as another sign."﴾ ﴿"So that We may show you some of Our greatest signs."﴾ ﴿"Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand my breast for me,"﴾ ﴿"and ease my task for me,"﴾ ﴿"and untie the knot from my tongue,"﴾ ﴿"that they may understand my speech."﴾ ﴿"And appoint for me a minister from my family,"﴾ ﴿"Aaron, my brother."﴾ ﴿"Strengthen my back through him,"﴾ ﴿"and make him a partner in my affair,"﴾ ﴿"that we may glorify You much"﴾ ﴿"and remember You much."﴾ ﴿"Indeed You are ever Seeing of us."﴾

When Allah, blessed and exalted, willed to train him in receiving prophethood and its obligations, He commanded him to throw down the staff. Moses (peace be upon him) threw it down, and Allah altered its attributes and functions. It had been a staff with two prongs, and the two prongs became its mouth. It became a snake "moving swiftly," meaning it moved, walked, and seized stones in its mouth. When Moses (peace be upon him) saw it, he saw it as a marvel, so he turned and fled without looking back. Allah said to him, "Seize it and do not fear." This was because he sensed fear within himself, meaning that what afflicts humans befell him. It is reported that Moses (peace be upon him) grasped it with the sleeves of his robe, so he was forbidden from doing that. He then took it in his hand, and it became a staff as it had been the first time, and this is "its original form."

Then Allah, exalted, commanded him to draw his hand to his side, and "side" here is the "wing" (janah), used metaphorically and figuratively. From this is the verse of the rajaz poet:

> "I press it to my chest and wing."

Some people say that "janah" means the hand.

All of this is correct according to the way of metaphor. Do you not see that Ja'far ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) was called "the one with two wings" because of his two hands, when the two wings were set in place of the two hands, being likened to the wing of a bird?

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Everyone who is frightened by darkness or something similar, when he presses his hand to his wing, his fright subsides and his heart is gathered. So Allah, blessed and exalted, combined for Moses (peace be upon him) the calming of fright together with the sign in the hand. It is reported that the hand of Moses (peace be upon him) came out white, shining and transparent, as if it were a sun.

His saying: ﴿without harm﴾ means: without leprosy or disfigurement, but rather it is something that recedes and returns according to the need for it. His saying: ﴿so that We may show you some of Our greatest signs﴾ may mean that the signs are described as "great," as in the earlier verse ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:8) and ﴿other uses﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:18), and similar. It may also mean specifying these two verses as the greatest of the signs, as if He said: "so that We may show you the greatest of Our signs." Thus both meanings are possible.

Then He, blessed and exalted, commanded him to go to Pharaoh, who, according to some of what has been said, was Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, though other things have been said, and none of that is authentic. The word "transgressed" (taghā) means that he exceeded the limit in corruption.

(p. 91) His saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand my breast for me"﴾ and the verse that follows: when Allah, exalted, commanded him to go to Pharaoh, he knew that this was the message and understood the weight of the obligation, so he asked Allah for help, for he has no power except through Him. His saying ﴿expand my breast for me﴾ means: so that I may understand what comes to me of matters. The "knot" that he asked to have untied was the one that had afflicted him from the live coal that he put in his mouth when Pharaoh tested him. It is reported regarding this that Pharaoh wanted to kill him when he was a child, when he reached out his hand to Pharaoh's beard. His wife said to him, "He does not understand." He said, "No, he understands, and he is my enemy." She said, "Let us test him." He said, "Do it." So she brought some live coals of fire and a tray containing rubies. He said, "If he takes the rubies, we will know that he understands; if he takes the fire, we will excuse him." Moses reached out his hand to a live coal and took it, and it did not harm his hand. He put it in his mouth, and it burned him and left a knot in his tongue in his old age, meaning an impediment that obscured some of the letters. Ibn al-Jawhari (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Allah withheld the fire from his hand so that the fire would not say, "This is my nature," and He burned his tongue so that Moses would not say, "This is my position." Moses (peace be upon him) only sought from the untying of the knot the degree that would allow him to understand speech. It is therefore possible that all of that was removed, and it is possible that a little of it remained. Thus it is consistent that he was granted his request and that Pharaoh said: ﴿and he can hardly speak clearly﴾ (Az-Zukhruf 43:52). Had we supposed that it was entirely removed, Pharaoh's words would have been an insult to Moses (peace be upon him) because of his former condition.

The "minister" (wazīr) is the helper who bears the burden of affairs, and "wizr" is their weight. The phrase may be understood as requesting a minister from his family in general, and then Aaron was specified as the minister sought. It may also mean: "make Aaron a minister," since he began the request with him, and in this case the first object of the verb "make" (ij'al) is Aaron. Aaron (peace be upon him) was four years older than Moses.

Ibn 'Amir alone read ﴿ashdud﴾ with a fatḥa on the hamza and ﴿ushrikhu﴾ with a ḍamma on the hamza, on the basis that Moses (peace be upon him) attributed these verbs to himself. Here the imperative does not intend prophethood, but rather his management and efforts, because prophethood cannot be shared by Moses (peace be upon him) with any human. The rest read ﴿ushdud﴾ with a ḍamma on the hamza and ﴿wa-ashrik﴾ as a supplication for strengthening his back and making Aaron (peace be upon him) a partner in prophethood. This is the preferred reading, because it fits the supplication mentioned before, and other verses that indicate his request for Aaron's confirmation of him support it.

Al-azr (the back) means the back, as Abu 'Ubayda said. It is as if he said: "Strengthen my help through him, and make him my supporter in what I attempt of affairs." Imru' al-Qays said:

> "In a bend where its plants have supported the straying, the passage of armies, victorious and defeated."

That is, it supported it and grew to its height.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir pronounced the yā' in ﴿akhī﴾ with a fatḥa, while the rest made it sukūn. It is reported from Nafi' the reading ﴿wa-ashrikhu-hu﴾ with an added waw in pronunciation after the hā'. Then Moses (peace be upon him) made what he requested of the blessings of Allah, exalted, a cause that obliges much worship and diligence in the affair of Allah. His saying ﴿kathīran﴾ ("much") is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, whose implied sense is: "glorification much."

﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Musa."﴾ ﴿And We had already bestowed a favour upon you at another time,﴾ ﴿when We inspired your mother with what was inspired:﴾ ﴿"Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and the river will throw him onto the bank, and an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him." And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you might be reared under My eye.﴾

The meaning: Allah the Exalted said, "You have been given, O Musa, what you asked for: the expansion of your breast, the easing of your affair, and the untying of the knot of your tongue, either in its entirety or to the extent needed in your actions." The granting of this request is a favour from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. He then joined to it the earlier favour He had shown him, by way of drawing his attention to it, so that his striving would grow greater and his insight would be strengthened.

Regarding the story of Musa, peace be upon him, as it has been narrated: Pharaoh was told that the ruin of his kingdom would come at the hands of a boy from the Children of Israel. So he ordered that every male child born to the Children of Israel be killed. Then he saw, along with the people of his realm, that the annihilation of the Children of Israel would harm the Copts, since they were the labourers of the land, the craftsmen, and the like. So he resolved to kill the boys for one year and to spare them for one year. Harun, peace be upon him, was born in the year of sparing, and his mother was Amina. Then Musa, peace be upon him, was born in the fourth year of the killing, and his mother feared for him from slaughter, so she remained anxious. Then Allah inspired her, it is said through an angel who came to her, informed her and commanded her. Some of those who related this said: she was not a prophetess, because we find in the Law and its transmissions that angels have spoken to those who were not prophets. Others said: rather, the mother of Musa was a prophetess, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, by this inspiration. Others said: rather, this inspiration was a dream she saw in sleep. A group said: rather, it was inspiration of inner suggestion and guidance, like the inspiration of Allah to the bee and others. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, inspired her until she made a chest and placed Musa in it, lying on a bedding, and then cast him into the Nile river. Pharaoh was sitting in a place overlooking the Nile when he saw the chest. He ordered it brought to him, with his wife with him. He opened it and saw him. His wife took pity on him and asked for him to adopt him as a son, and he permitted her that. It is also narrated that the chest came on the water to the landing place where the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife drew water. They took the chest and carried it to her. She opened it and informed Pharaoh, and asked him for him. Then she offered him for nursing, but he would not accept any woman. So they called out for him in the city, and he was taken around and presented to the wet-nurses, but whenever a woman was presented to him, he refused her. His mother, when he had gone from her into the Nile, remained grief-stricken, her heart empty except for her concern for him. She said to his sister: "Seek his trace in the city, perhaps some news of him will reach us." Then while the sister was going about, she caught sight of him and understood his situation. She said to them: "I will direct you to a household that will take charge of him for you, and they will be sincere toward him." They seized her and said to her: "Do you know this child?" She said: "No, but I know of the people of this house their eagerness to draw near to the queen and their striving in her service and in pleasing her." They left her and asked her for the guidance, so she brought Musa's mother. When she brought him near, he took her breast, and Asiya, Pharaoh's wife, was delighted. She said to her: "Stay with me in the palace." She replied: "I would not leave my house and my child, but he may stay with me." So she treated the people of that house with the utmost kindness. The Children of Israel took pride in this nursing and in the connection to the queen. Musa remained until he completed his nursing. Then Asiya sent to her: "Bring my child on such-and-such day," and she commanded her servants and attendants to meet him with gifts, presents and clothing. He arrived to her in the best condition and the most beautiful youth. She was delighted with him and entered upon Pharaoh so that he might see him and love him. He saw him, was pleased with him, and brought him close. Then Musa, peace be upon him, seized the beard of Pharaoh and pulled it. Pharaoh flared up and said: "This is an enemy of mine," and ordered his killing. His wife pleaded with him concerning him and said: "He does not understand." Pharaoh said: "Rather, he understands." So they agreed upon a test with a live coal and a ruby, as we mentioned just above in the untying of the knot. Allah rescued him from Pharaoh and returned him to his mother. He grew up with her until he matured. He was a strong and virtuous youth, and the Children of Israel took pride in him through the outward appearance of that nursing. He would protect them, and his side was with them, while he knew of himself that he was one of them and of their pure lineage. His insight was in protecting them, and the notables of the Children of Israel knew this about him.

Then the story of the Copt who was fighting with an Israelite came down, and its mention is comprehensively given in its place. So Musa, peace be upon him, left Egypt until he reached Madyan. What happened between him and Shu'ayb, the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, is comprehensively stated in its own place, namely that he married his younger daughter in return for tending the sheep for ten years. Then he resolved to travel with his wife to the land of Egypt. On his way he went astray on a dark night and saw a fire, as has been mentioned earlier. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, enumerated for Musa in this verse what this story contained of Allah's gentleness toward him in every grace, and His rescuing him from one trial to another. And these were the trials (futun) with which He tested him, that is, He tried him and purified him until he became fit for prophethood and was sound for it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿mā yūḥā﴾ ("that which was inspired"), is an indefinite expression that conveys the greatness and magnitude of the matter among the favours. This is like His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿idh yaghsha al-sidrata mā yaghshā﴾ ("when there covered the lote-tree that which covered it") [al-Najm: 16]. It is frequent in the Qur'an and in speech. The phrase ﴿an iqdhifīhi﴾ ("that you cast him") is a substitute (badal) for "mā" (the indefinite). The first pronoun in "iqdhīhi" refers to Musa, and the second refers to the chest. It is permissible for the second to refer to Musa, peace be upon him. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿falyulqihi al-yammu﴾ ("let the river throw him up") is a report that comes in the form of a command, for emphasis, since a command is the most decisive and binding of verbal forms (ṣīgha). Among this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Stand up, and I will pray for you for you," where a statement was given in the form of a command about himself, for emphasis. This is frequent. Since the verb has come in the manner of a command, its response is likewise fine. The "enemy" who was an enemy of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and of Musa, peace be upon him, is Pharaoh. But the mother of Musa reported him by way of ambiguity, and for this reason she said to his sister: "Follow him," while she did not know where he was.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with a trial. So you remained years among the people of Madyan. Then you came [here] at a appointed time, O Musa.﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself.﴾

The governing element of "idh" (when) is a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "And We bestowed favor when..." The interpretation of this verse has already been explained in the account mentioned just above.

A group read "kay taqarra" (that she might be cooled) with a fatha on the qaf, and a group read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf. The soul he killed was the soul of the Egyptian (al-Qibti) who was fighting the Israelite; Musa struck him (fawakazahu) and thereby brought about his death. Al-ghamm ("distress") means the anguish of the soul; Musa, peace be upon him, was distressed because of a command concerning one who sought him so that he might take revenge on him.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We tested you with a trial﴾, its meaning is: We freed you with a thorough deliverance. This is the saying of the majority of the exegetes. A group said its meaning is: We examined you by testing. According to this interpretation, only that with which Musa, peace be upon him, was tested after his reaching maturity and being charged with obligations is intended, and what came before that does not fall within the testing of Musa, peace be upon him.

The number of his years among the people of Madyan is ten years, because he only fulfilled the better of the two terms.

As for His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿according to a decree﴾, it means: at a fixed appointed time for the prophethood which Allah has willed for you. From this is the saying of the poet:

He attained the caliphate when it was for him a decree,
just as Musa came to his Lord at an appointed time.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have chosen you for Myself﴾, its meaning is: We made you the place of favor and the seat of kindness and beneficence. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 40–41:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We delivered you from distress and tested you with a trial. So you remained years among the people of Madyan. Then you came [here] at a appointed time, O Musa.﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself.﴾

The governing element of "idh" (when) is a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "And We bestowed favor when..." The interpretation of this verse has already been explained in the account mentioned just above.

A group read "kay taqarra" (that she might be cooled) with a fatha on the qaf, and a group read "kay taqirra" with a kasra on the qaf. The soul he killed was the soul of the Egyptian (al-Qibti) who was fighting the Israelite; Musa struck him (fawakazahu) and thereby brought about his death. Al-ghamm ("distress") means the anguish of the soul; Musa, peace be upon him, was distressed because of a command concerning one who sought him so that he might take revenge on him.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and We tested you with a trial﴾, its meaning is: We freed you with a thorough deliverance. This is the saying of the majority of the exegetes. A group said its meaning is: We examined you by testing. According to this interpretation, only that with which Musa, peace be upon him, was tested after his reaching maturity and being charged with obligations is intended, and what came before that does not fall within the testing of Musa, peace be upon him.

The number of his years among the people of Madyan is ten years, because he only fulfilled the better of the two terms.

As for His saying, blessed and exalted is He, ﴿according to a decree﴾, it means: at a fixed appointed time for the prophethood which Allah has willed for you. From this is the saying of the poet:

He attained the caliphate when it was for him a decree,
just as Musa came to his Lord at an appointed time.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and I have chosen you for Myself﴾, its meaning is: We made you the place of favor and the seat of kindness and beneficence. His saying "for Myself" is an idafa of honor, like your saying "the House of Allah" and similar. "And fasting is for Me, and I shall reward it" [a hadith]. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 42–46:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.﴾ ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh, for he has indeed transgressed.﴾ ﴿Speak to him gently; perhaps he may take heed or fear.﴾ ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ ﴿He said: "Do not fear; indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing."﴾

God Most High commanded Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, in this verse to proceed to the call to Pharaoh. He addressed Moses alone as an honour to him, and it is possible that Aaron was also inspired, together with a king, to carry it out. "With My signs" means: with My indications which I have given you, of miracles, signs of revelation, and commands and prohibitions such as the Torah. "Taniya" means: you should weaken and slacken. It is said: "Fulan slackened (wana) in such-and-such a matter" when he delayed in it out of weakness. From this is the saying of the poet:

﴿...............................﴾ "So I am not one who slackens, nor a weak and inexperienced youth."

And al-wana is fatigue and failure, in animals and humans. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "and do not be feeble (wa la tahina) in My remembrance," meaning: do not become soft, from your saying: "hayyin layyin" (gentle, soft).

As for "the gentle word," one group said: its meaning is to use kunya (polite indirect address) with him. Another group said: rather, He commanded them to beautify the word.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is the correct view, because whoever wishes to call a person to a matter he dislikes, the proper course is that he should make clear in his expression the meaning he intends, so that he does not confuse it or deviate from it; then after that he should strive for his expression to be gracious and his address to be gentle, for that is more attractive to the intended goal. So God Most High commanded Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, to follow with Pharaoh the completion of the call with gentleness of speech.

His saying "perhaps" (la'alla) means: in accordance with your hope and expectation. So the expectation in it refers only to the side of the humans. The majority read "yafruta" with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the ra, and its meaning is: he hastens and rushes to do harm to us. From it comes "al-farit" in water, which is the one who goes ahead of the people to it. The poet said:

﴿...﴾ "They hastened against us, and they were of our companions, as the forerunners (furat) precede the drinkers (wurrad)."

(p-98) Another group said: "yufrita" with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the ra, and its meaning is: he exceeds the limit. Ibn Muhaysin read: "yufrata" with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the ra, and its meaning is that some bearer compels him to hasten toward us.

His Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed I am with you﴾ means: with help, support, and power over Pharaoh. This is like when you say: "The commander is with so-and-so," if you mean that he protects him. "Hearing and seeing" are two expressions for the perception by which nothing hidden is concealed. Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 47–49:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿So go to him and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace is upon those who follow guidance."﴾ ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away.﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Who then is the Lord of you two, O Moses?"﴾

The meaning: Go to Pharaoh and inform him that you two are messengers to him. He addressed Pharaoh as "your Lord" to belittle him, since he claimed lordship. Then they were commanded to call him to send the Children of Israel with them and to free them from the humiliation of serving the Copts. The call to faith has already been mentioned in this verse, and this is the full extent of what Pharaoh was called to: "faith and the sending of the Children of Israel." It is apparent that their mission to him was not of the same nature as the sending to the Children of Israel. The torment of the Children of Israel was the slaughter of their sons and their humiliation. The "sign" to which they referred is the staff and the hand. He said, "We have come to you" — while the one who brought it was Moses — as a figurative usage, since both of them were messengers.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And peace is upon those who follow guidance﴾, it is possible that this is the final statement and its conclusion, so "peace" may well mean a greeting, as if they were turning away from him with it, and in keeping with the custom of giving salutation at the end of speech, they greeted those who follow guidance. In this there is a rebuke.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this understanding, people use this verse in their addresses and dialogues. It is also possible that it is part of the continuing speech, connected to His words, Glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾. On this reading it could be a report that safety belongs to those who are guided. Each of these two meanings has been stated by a group, but without this summary. Some said "peace" means "safety," and "upon" means "for" (the particle lam), i.e., peace is for those who follow guidance.

(p-99) When they finished the statement they had been commanded to make, [and it ended] with His words "and turns away," Pharaoh addressed them both. In the narration of this verse there is an omission that the apparent meaning of the speech indicates; its implied sense is: They came to him, and when they had said all that they were commanded to say, Pharaoh said to them: "Who then is your Lord?" His words "O Moses," after he had joined Aaron with him in the pronoun, are a call meant for specification and focusing attention, since he was the bearer of the great message and the one entrusted with the clear signs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 50–52:

The words of the Most High:

﴿He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided [it]."﴾ ﴿He said, "Then what is the state of the former generations?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾

Musa (peace be upon him) took the answer into his own hands, from the point where [Pharaoh] had singled him out in the question. Then he informed him of the attributes of Allah that are not shared with Pharaoh in any way, nor by any figurative meaning. The exegetes differed concerning His words: ﴿who gave everything its creation﴾. One group said: Allah gave the male of every animal its kind and its form, [namely] the female, then guided it to mating. Another group said: Allah gave every existing thing among His creatures its creation and its form, meaning He perfected that for it and made it excellent; then "guided" means: He made every thing easy for its benefits and its necessities.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement is more noble in meaning and more general over all existing things.

A group read "khalqahu" (its creation) with a fatha on the lam, and the second object of "a'ta" (gave) would then be understood as implied, its estimate being: its perfection or its welfare.

As for Pharaoh's words: ﴿Then what is the state of the former generations?﴾, it is possible that he meant to dispute with [Musa] according to what had preceded of the speech and to contradict him in it. On this view, it is not appropriate that he meant anything other than: "What is the state of the former generations, that they were not resurrected and your command was not found among them?" Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 53–56:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle, and threaded for you therein roads, and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants.﴾ ﴿Eat and graze your livestock. Surely in that are signs for people of intellect.﴾ ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more.﴾ ﴿And We certainly showed him all Our signs, but he denied and refused.﴾

Consider these things which Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned: they are of the kind that the primary intellects judge Pharaoh and every human to be far from. For if he had said: "He is the Provider, the Capable, the Willing, the Knowing," and similar expressions, it would have been possible for Pharaoh to deceive and say: "I do all of this." Rather, Musa (peace be upon him) brought attributes which Pharaoh could not claim for himself.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Abbas read "mihadan" with a kasra on the mim and an alif, and "al-mihad" is the plural of "mahd" (cradle); it was also said that it is a singular noun, like "farsh" and "firash." 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "mahdan" with a fatha on the mim and a sukun on the ha'. His saying "salaka" means: "nahaja" and "laHaba" (he made a path). "As-subul" means the paths (ṭuruq). His saying "fa-akhrajna bihi" may be the words of Musa (peace be upon him), with the implied meaning: "Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: 'fa-akhrajna.'" It may also be that the speech of Musa ended at His saying "wa-anzala min as-sama'i ma'an," and then Allah, the Exalted, connected the speech of Musa by informing Muhammad (ﷺ). The intended meaning is the whole creation through these signs that were pointed out. "Al-azwaj" means "al-anwa'" (kinds), and His saying "shatta" is an adjective for "al-azwaj," meaning: diverse.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Eat and graze your livestock﴾ means: they are suitable that some of them be eaten and that sheep graze in them. The expression was put in the form of a command because it is the most gentle of actions and the most soothing to the souls. "An-nuha" is the plural of "nuhya," and "an-nuhya" is the intellect that restrains from vile things.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿From it We created you﴾, i.e., from the earth, and this is in reference to Adam (peace be upon him) having been created from dust. His saying: ﴿and into it We will return you﴾ means: by death and burial, or by perishing however it occurs. His saying: ﴿and from it We will bring you forth﴾ means: by resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And We certainly showed him Our signs﴾ is information from Allah, the Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ) about Pharaoh. This supports that the speech from His saying "fa-akhrajna bihi" is directed to Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying "kulluha" refers to the signs which he saw, not that he saw every sign of Allah; rather the meaning is that Allah showed him certain signs, namely the staff, the hand, the plague of darkness, and other things, and his seeing of these signs was comprehensive, seeing them all in their completeness, as if He said: "We certainly showed him Our signs in their entirety." He attributed the signs to the pronoun of majesty to honour them. His, the Exalted, saying: "wa-aba" necessitates that Pharaoh acquired (his disbelief), and this is what reward and punishment depend upon.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 57–59:

His, Exalted and Majestic is He, saying:

﴿They said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?"﴾ ﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it. So set between us and you a appointment which neither we nor you will fail to keep, at a place equitable (suwan).﴾ ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the Day of Adornment, and that the people be gathered at mid-morning."﴾

This dialogue from Pharaoh indicates that the matter of Moses, peace be upon him, had grown strong, that many of the Children of Israel had followed him, and that his affair had taken hold in people's hearts. This is because it is the dialogue of one who needs proof, not of one who proclaims his own cause. "Their land" is the land of Egypt.

A group read "لا نَخْلُفُهُ" (lā nakhlufuhu) with a damma on the lām, and a group read "لا نَخْلُفْهُ" (lā nakhlufhu) with a sukūn on the lām, as a response to the imperative (jawāb al-amr). "Naḥnu" (we) is an emphatic addition to the pronoun, since the speech required the coordination (ʿaṭf) upon it to be emphasized. "Maw'idan" (an appointment) is the first object of "ijʿal" (make), and "makānan" (a place) is the second object. This is what Abū ʿAlī (al-Fārisī) chose, and he prohibited "makānan" from being governed by "maw'idan," because the latter has been described (by a qualifier), and these nouns that function as verbs, when they are qualified, or coordinated upon, or have a predicate stated about them, or are diminutivised, or pluralised, and have become fully nominal in this manner, do not govern, and nothing that belongs to them is attached to them. The adverbs may be given broader scope so that they are attached after what we have mentioned, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will be called: "The hatred of God is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were called to faith and you disbelieved."﴾ [Ghafir: 10]. So His saying "idh" (when) is attached to "la-maqtu Allah" (the hatred of God), and he has stated about it, and this is permitted only with adverbs specifically. Likewise, Abū ʿAlī prohibited that "makānan" be put in the accusative as an adverb substituting for the object.

(p-103) The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In this there is consideration. A group prohibited that "makānan" be in the accusative as the second object of "nukhlifuhu," while a number of grammarians permitted it, and its rationale is that the scope is broadened to include failing the appointment. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read "سِوًى" (siwan) with a kasra on the sīn, while ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamza read "سُوًى" (suwan) with a damma on it. The majority pronounced the nūn with tanwīn. al-Ḥasan read "سِوى" (siwa) with a kasra on the sīn without tanwīn. Abū al-Fatḥ said: leaving out the tanwīn here is problematic, and what should be preferred is that it is treated as a pause (waqf). A group read "سَواءً" (sawāʾan), which Abū ʿAmr mentioned from Ibn Abī ʿAylah. The meaning of "siwā" is: equitably and fairly. Abū ʿAlī said: it is as if he said: a place near to us, as near to you as it is to us.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

He only meant: our state in it is equal, so that this nearness is general, and that the positions in it are one in the pursuit of truth, i.e., your leadership will not stand in the way of it, and only the proof is sought. "Suwan" is a dialect form of "siwā," and from this word is the saying of the poet:

؎ Indeed our father had settled in a town, suwan, between Qays of ʿAylān and the Fizr.

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

And he has succeeded today who prevails.﴾

The meaning: The sorcerers were gathered, and he (Pharaoh) promised them and ordered them to prepare against Moses. This is "his scheme." Then Pharaoh came with his assembly and the people of his state, and the sorcerers were with him. They were a band whom Allah, Exalted, had not created more skilled in magic. Moses, peace be upon him, also came with the Children of Israel. Moses, peace be upon him, said to the sorcerers, "Woe to you!" This is the address of one who warns. In this verse he urged them to speak the truth when they see it, and not to confound (the truth) with falsehood.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, along with Nafiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿĀmir, recited: "fa-yasḥitakum" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim recited: "fa-yusḥitakum" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ. Both are two dialectal forms with one meaning: it is said saḥita and asḥita, meaning "he destroyed and eliminated." From this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"The bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left of wealth nothing but what is stripped bare or cut off."

So this is from asḥita.

When the sorcerers heard this statement, this speech alarmed them, and a severe terror fell into their souls from his awesomeness. They disputed about their affair. The word "tanāzuʿ" (disputing) implies a disagreement that existed among them in secret; that is, some said to others: "He is right," and some said: "He is a liar," and some said: "If it is from Allah, He will overcome us," and similar statements which are customary from large crowds at times of fear, such as in war and the like. It is known that all their private conferring was about the matter of Moses, peace be upon him. A group said: their private conferring was only about the verse that follows this, "Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers."

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The more apparent view is that this was said openly, for if their conferring had been that, there would have been no dispute. The word "najwā" means secret speech and private conversation; that is, each man conferred with the one beside him. Then they made that secret out of fear of Pharaoh, lest he perceive weakness in them, because at that time they were not determined to overcome Moses, peace be upon him, but it was merely a suspicion on the part of some of them.

His Exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ and so on. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī recited: "inna" with a shaddah on the nūn, "hadhāni" with an alif and a light nūn as the dual marker. Abu ʿAmr alone recited: "inna hadhayni la-sāḥirāni." Ibn Kathir recited: "in hadhānni la-sāḥirāni," with the nūn of "in" lightened and the nūn of "hadhānni" shaddah, "la-saḥarān." Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim recited: "in" light, "hadhāni" also light, "la-sāḥirāni." A group recited: "in hadhāni illā sāḥirān"; a group recited: "in dhān la-sāḥirān"; a group recited: "mā hadhāni illā sāḥirān"; and a group recited: "in hadhānn" with a shaddah on the nūn of "hadhānn."

As for the first reading, one group said: "inna" here means "yes," as it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in his sermon: "Inni al-ḥamda lillāh" with the raising of "al-ḥamd." ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "in wa-rākibuhā" when a man said to him: "May Allah curse the she-camel that carried me to you." This interpretation includes that the lām does not enter the predicate of the inchoative, which is permissible in poetry, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"Umm al-Ḥulays is indeed an old woman of the sort, content with meat as the bone of the neck."

A group went to the view that this verse is in the dialect of the Banu al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, which is retaining the dual alif in the accusative and genitive cases. From this is the verse of the poet:

"He struck between his ears with a thrust that called him to the dust of the desert, a barren one."

And the verse of another:

"He lowered his gaze like the lowering of the brave one, and if he saw an opening, the brave one's fangs would have struck it."

This dialect is attributed to Kinanah and attributed to Khathʿam. Al-Farrāʾ said: the alif in "hadhān" is a support and is not added for the dual; rather it is the alif of "hadhā" which was left in the dual state, just as we say "alladhī," then in the plural we add a nūn and leave the yāʾ in the accusative, nominative, and genitive states. Al-Zajjāj said: in the speech there is a pronoun whose estimate is: "innahu hadhāni la-sāḥirāni" (indeed it, these two are certainly sorcerers).

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this interpretation there is the entry of the lām into the predicate. Some grammarians said: the alif of "hadhān" here is likened to the alif of "taf'alān." Ibn Kaysan said: since "hadhā" has one form in its nominative, accusative, and genitive, its dual is left in this way here. A group, among them ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and Abu ʿAmr, said: this is among what the scribe erred in and was corrected with the correct form, which is the lightening of the nūn of "in."

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These views are open to objection, except what has been said that it is a dialect, and "in" meaning "ajal" (indeed/yes) and "nam," or that "in" in the speech is a pronoun.

As for those who read "in" light, it is, according to Sibawayh, the light form of the heavy (inna), and the noun after it is nominative. Al-Farrāʾ says: it has the meaning of "mā" (not), and the lām has the meaning of "illā" (except). The reasoning for the other readings is clear.

Many of the exegetes rendered "al-ṭarīqa" (the way of life) as "al-sāda" (the nobles), but what is intended is the people of intellect, age, and wisdom. It is related that the Arabs say: "fulān ṭarīqat qawmihi," meaning their leader. The more apparent meaning of "al-ṭarīqa" here is that it is the course of life, the dominion, and the state in which they are. "Al-muthlā" is the feminine of "amthal," meaning the superior and good one.

The majority of reciters recited: "fa-ajmaʿū" with a cutting alif and a kasra on the mīm, in the sense of "resolve." Abu ʿAmr alone recited: "fa-ajmiʿū" from "jammaʿa," meaning: combine your magic, some of it with others. Ibn Kathir recited: "thumma" with a fatḥa on the mīm, "ītū" with a sukūn on the yāʾ; he also recited, in the narration of Shibl from him: "thumu ītū" with a kasra on both. Abu ʿAlī said: this is an error, and there is no basis for a kasra on the mīm of "thumma." The majority recited: "thumma i'tū" with a fatḥa on the mīm and a hamza after the alif. His Exalted saying: ﴿ṣaffan﴾ is a circumstantial accusative, meaning: lined up in rows, and they summoned one another to this because it is more awe-inspiring and more visible to them. "Aflaḥa" means: he attained his desire, and "istaʿlā": sought loftiness in his affair and strove in its striving.

The majority of reciters read "talaqqaf" with a jazm and a shadda on the qaf, as a response to the imperative. Ibn 'Amir alone read "talaqqufa," which is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal); it may be from the thing thrown (al-mulqa) by extension, and it may be from the thing thrown, which is the staff; and this is a circumstantial clause even though it has not yet occurred, like His saying: ﴿hadyan baligha al-Ka'bah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], and this is common. Hafs from ʿAsim read "talqufu" with a sukun on the fa' and a lightening of the qaf, and he made the verb feminine while it is attributed to what is in the right hand, since the staff is intended by that. Al-Bazzi related from Ibn Kathir that he used to stress the fa' of "talaqqafa," as if he intended "tatalaqqafu," and then assimilated; Abu 'Ali rejected this reading.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that its reciter only maintains it in continuous recitation (wasl) where one can dispense with bringing in an alif. The majority read "kayadu" with a raf', and a group read "kayda" with a nasb. The latter is on the basis that "ma" is kafffa (a restrictive particle) and "kayda" is in the accusative governed by "sana'u" (they crafted); the raf' of "kayadu" is on the basis that "ma" carries the meaning of "alladhi" (that which). "Yuflihu" means: he remains and attains his aim; and a group said its meaning is that the magician is killed wherever he is found.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the recompense of one who lacks success. A group read "ayna ata" (wherever he comes), and the meaning of both is close.

It is related among the narratives of this verse that Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, sat in a raised chamber of his, eighty cubits long, while the people were below him in an open plain. The seventy thousand magicians came and threw down from their ropes and staffs what loaded three hundred camels, and the matter was alarming. Then Moses, peace be upon him, threw his staff from his hand, and it turned into a serpent, and began to grow, until it is narrated that it crossed the river with its tail, and it was said: the sea. Pharaoh, in the midst of this, was laughing and thought that the matter was settled. Then it came to devour the ropes and the staffs until it had consumed them, and it fled toward Pharaoh, so he was terrified at that and said: "O Moses!" Moses, peace be upon him, stretched out his hand toward it, and it returned to being a staff as it had been. The sorcerers looked, knew the truth, and saw the absence of the ropes and staffs, and so they believed, may Allah be pleased with them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 70–71:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting."﴾

Within this verse there is an implied elision (taqdir wa-hadhf, supposition and omission) indicated by the apparent wording. The implied part here is: "So Moses threw his staff, and it swallowed up all that they had brought," or something similar. It is narrated that when the magicians saw the staff, with no trace of magic in it, and then saw it transform into a serpent, devouring the ropes and staves, and then returning to its former state, with the ropes and staves gone, they became certain of the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, and that the matter was from Allah, the Exalted.

He placed "Aaron" before "Moses" so that the ends of the verses would be level (tastawi ru'us al-ayy), by transferring the meaning of the magicians' statement. This is like His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿pairs of various kinds of plants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 53], where the placing of "various" (shatta) later is only so that the ends of the verses are balanced. Likewise His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ [Ta-Ha: 129], where the placing of His saying "and a specified term" later is only so that the ends of the verses are level.

Ibn Kathir, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, and Warsh on the authority of Nafi' recited "āmantum" as a statement (khabar). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir recited "a-āmantum" with two hamzas (the interrogative form). His saying "before I gave you permission" is a sign of approach (muqarabah) on his part and a degree of acquiescence (idh'an). His saying "on alternate sides" means cutting off the right hand with the left foot. His saying "on the trunks of palm trees" is a broad usage (ittisa'), in that he is tied to the trunk; it is not in the sense of your saying "Zayd is in the house." The preposition "ʿalā" (on) is also suitable in this meaning, in that he is tied at its top; it is not in the sense of your saying "I rode on the horse." His saying "whose" (ayyuna) means himself and the Lord of Moses, peace be upon him. Al-Tabari said: he means himself and Moses, peace be upon him. The first view is more appropriate given the bluster of Pharaoh.

﴿They said: "We will never prefer you over the clear signs that have come to us, or over Him who originated us. So decree whatever you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us. God is better and more enduring."﴾

The magicians said to Pharaoh, because of what he was summoning them to, ﴿We will never prefer you﴾, meaning: we will never prefer you, or prefer safety from you, over the proof of God the Exalted and His manifest signs that we have seen, or over Him who originated us. This is according to a group who hold that the waw in His saying "and He who originated us" is conjunctive (ʿāṭifah). Another group said it is the waw of oath (wāw al-qasam), and "fatarana" means "created us and brought us into being." So do, Pharaoh, whatever you wish. Your decree is only in this worldly life, while the Hereafter belongs to us, with bliss, and to you, with punishment.

People differed over whether Pharaoh's threat was carried out against these magicians. One group said: he crucified them on palm trunks as he had said, so that the people became magicians in the morning and martyrs by evening, through God's kindness and mercy. Another group said: Pharaoh did not do that, since God had promised Moses, peace be upon him, that he and those with him would be the victors.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: All of this is possible. The crucifixion of the magicians and the cutting of their hands does not preclude that Moses, peace be upon him, and those with him prevailed, except through the apparent generality (ʿumūm) of the statement, and the resolution of that is clear.

As for His saying ﴿and the magic to which you compelled us﴾, one group said they meant what he had joined them to, of opposing Moses, peace be upon him, and what he had driven them to of that. Another group said: rather, Pharaoh had long been taking the children of the people to teach them magic and compelling them to it, so the magicians pointed to that. Their saying ﴿God is better and more enduring﴾ is a reply to his saying ﴿Which of us is sterner in punishment and more enduring﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 74–76:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, then for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. And that is the reward of those who purify themselves.﴾

A group said: this verse in its entirety is from the words of the magicians to Pharaoh, by way of admonishing him and clarifying regarding what they had done. And another group said: rather, it is from the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to Muhammad (ﷺ), as a reminder of the ugliness of what Pharaoh did and the goodness of what the magicians did, and as an admonition and a warning. The mentioned story has included its example. The criminal is the one who has acquired crimes and sins. His saying: ﴿he will neither die therein nor live﴾ is specific to the disbeliever, for he is punished with a punishment that brings him to the point of death, then he is not finished off so that he may rest; rather his skin is restored and his punishment is renewed, so he does not live a pleasant life. As for those among the believers who enter the Fire because of sins, before the intercession takes them out, they are in a state of anguish, having come close to death, except that they are not finished off and their punishment is not renewed. This is the difference between them and the disbelievers. And in the authentic hadith: "They will be made to die a death," and this is its meaning, because he does not die in the Hereafter.

"The high ranks" are nearness to Allah, the Most High. And "tazakka" means: he obeyed Allah and adopted the best of matters. Reflect on the element of acquisition (taksub) in the word "tazakka," for it is clear.
