﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea. You will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid."﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his armies, and the sea covered them with what covered them.﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them.﴾

This is a resumption of narration about the affair of Musa. Between it and the earlier speech of the magicians lies a span of time in which events occurred to Musa and Pharaoh. When the affair of the magicians had ended, Musa had prevailed and his cause had grown strong, and Pharaoh promised him that he would send the Children of Israel with him. Musa, peace be upon him, remained faithful to this promise until Pharaoh betrayed him, broke his word, and informed him that he would not send them with him. Then Allah, exalted is He, sent the signs mentioned in other verses, such as the locusts, the lice, and so on to their end. Whenever a sign came, Pharaoh promised to send the Children of Israel once the punishment was lifted, but when it was lifted he broke his word, until another sign came. When the signs had run their course, Allah, exalted is He, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should leave Egypt with the Children of Israel by night, travelling (*sura*: travelling during the night). The word *"an"* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿an asri﴾ [p. 114] may be an explanatory particle (*mufassira*) with no place in the grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-ntalaqa al-mala'u minhum ani mshu﴾ [Sad: 6]. It may also be the particle that governs verbs (*al-nasiba lil-af'al*), in which case it occupies a position in the accusative after *awhayna* ("We revealed"). His saying "with My servants" is an honorific attribution (*idafat tashrif*) to the Children of Israel, since all creation are servants of Allah, but this is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-nafakhtu fihi min ruhi﴾ [al-Hijr: 29].

Among the accounts reported concerning this verse is that when Musa, peace be upon him, informed the Children of Israel of the night of departure, they borrowed jewellery and clothing from their acquaintances among the Copts. It is also reported that Musa, peace be upon him, gave them permission to do so and said to them: "Allah will bestow it upon you as a spoil." It is also reported that they did this without his opinion, and this latter is more fitting for him, peace be upon him. What will come in the discussion on the plural of *huli* (jewellery) supports this. It is also reported that the Children of Israel kneaded their provisions on the night of their journey and set them aside to rise, but Musa, peace be upon him, hastened them in departing, so they cooked it unleavened (*fatir*). Hence it became their custom at that time of year, down to *halumma* (to this day). It is also reported that Musa, peace be upon him, set out with the Children of Israel, who numbered six hundred thousand people, travelling from Egypt intending the Qalzam Sea (the Red Sea). News reached Pharaoh, so he gathered his armies, mustered them, and set out after him. Then Allah revealed to Musa that he should head for the sea. The Children of Israel panicked, seeing the enemy behind them and the sea in front of them, while Musa, peace be upon him, trusted in the handiwork of Allah, exalted is He. When Pharaoh saw them heading toward the sea, he became covetous of them, and their destination was a place where the open plains and wide roads come to an end. People differed about the number of Pharaoh's army. It was said that his horses numbered seventy thousand dark-coloured steeds, with a proportionate number of other colours. It was also said to be more than this, but I have omitted it because of its weak authenticity. When Musa reached the sea and Pharaoh drew near to overtake him, and the fear of the Children of Israel grew intense, Allah, blessed and exalted is He, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should strike the sea with his staff. It is reported that the revelation concerning this had come while he was still in Egypt, which is the apparent meaning of the verse. It is also reported that the revelation concerning this came only at the place of the event itself. The discourse in this verse proceeds by way of describing the situation and joining some matters to others. Musa, peace be upon him, struck the sea, and it split into twelve parts, wide paths with walls of standing water between them. After Allah, exalted is He, had sent the east wind (*rih al-saba*), which dried those paths until they became dry, Musa, peace be upon him, entered, and the Children of Israel entered. Pharaoh reached the entrance while all the Children of Israel were in the sea, and he saw the water in that state. His people panicked and considered the matter monstrous. He said to them, may Allah curse him: "It split only out of awe of me." Here lies the full extent of his misguidance of them. Allah drove him to enter. Jibril, peace be upon him, came riding a female horse and went before Pharaoh's horse, and the people followed him until they were all completely in the sea, and it closed over them. The Children of Israel heard the water closing, and they had all come out of the sea, so they were amazed. Musa, peace be upon him, informed them that Pharaoh and his people had perished in it, so they asked for proof of this. The sea then cast up the bodies of the people, and Allah, exalted is He, placed Pharaoh upon a raised ground with his well-known coat of mail.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the summary of the narratives of this verse according to its wording, and the affair of Pharaoh has already been treated more fully than this in a place where it was required.

His saying, exalted is He, "*yabsan*" (dry) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as a description. Some people read it as "*yabisan*" (dry, with the active form), and al-Zajjaj referred to this reading. Hamza alone read "*la takhaf*" (you shall not fear) as a jussive, either as a response to the imperative, or as a separate prohibition. The majority of readers (*al-jumhur*) read "*la takhafu*" (you fear not), and this is on the basis that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to Musa, peace be upon him. It may also be a description of the path, with the implied sense "you will not fear in it," that is, it will have this quality. The meaning of this statement is: you will not fear being overtaken by Pharaoh and his armies, nor will you dread drowning in the sea. Abu 'Amr, as reported from him, read "*fa-ttaba'ahum*" with a doubled *ta'*. The verb *tabi'a* and *ittaba'a* only take one direct object, as in your saying: *shawaytu* and *ishtawaytu* (I roasted), *fadaytu* and *if-tadaytu* (I ransomed), *hafartu* and *ihtafartu* (I dug). His saying "*bi-junudihi*" (with his armies) either has the *ba'* together with what it governs in a circumstantial position, as when you say: "Zayd went out with his weapon," or it serves to make the verb transitive to a second object, since it does not take an object without a preposition except one. The majority read "*fa-atba'ahum*" with a sukun on the *ta'*, and this verb takes two objects. On this basis, the *ba'* is either superfluous, the sense being: "Pharaoh made his army follow them," or it is the *ba'* of circumstance, and the second object is understood, as if you had said: "his leaders" or "his resolve" or something similar. The first is more apparent. A group read "*fa-ghashiyahum*" and another group read "*fa-ghashshahumu Allah*" (Allah covered them). His saying ﴿ma ghashiyahum﴾ [what covered them] is an expression of vagueness that is more terrifying than stating a specific measure, and this is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿idh yaghsha al-sidrata ma yaghsha﴾ [al-Najm: 16].

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-adalla fir'awnu qawmahu﴾ [And Pharaoh led his people astray] means: from the beginning of his affair until this end. Then He emphasised, exalted is He, with His saying ﴿wa-ma hada﴾ [and did not guide them], as a contrast to Pharaoh's saying, may Allah curse him: ﴿wa-ma uhdikum illa sabila al-rashad﴾ [I show you nothing but the way of right guidance] [Ghafir: 29].

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea. When Pharaoh saw them heading toward the sea, he became covetous of them, and their destination was a place where the open plains and wide roads come to an end. People differed about the number of Pharaoh's army. It was said that his horses numbered seventy thousand dark-coloured steeds, with a proportionate number of other colours. It was also said to be more than this, but I have omitted it because of its weak authenticity. When Musa reached the sea and Pharaoh drew near to overtake him, and the fear of the Children of Israel grew intense, Allah, blessed and exalted is He, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should strike the sea with his staff. It is reported that the revelation concerning this had come while he was still in Egypt, which is the apparent meaning of the verse. It is also reported that the revelation concerning this came only at the place of the event itself. The discourse in this verse proceeds by way of describing the situation and joining some matters to others. Musa, peace be upon him, struck the sea, and it split into twelve parts, wide paths with walls of standing water between them. After Allah, exalted is He, had sent the east wind (*rih al-saba*), which dried those paths until they became dry, Musa, peace be upon him, entered, and the Children of Israel entered. Pharaoh reached the entrance while all the Children of Israel were in the sea, and he saw the water in that state. His people panicked and considered the matter monstrous. He said to them, may Allah curse him: "It split only out of awe of me." Here lies the full extent of his misguidance of them. Allah drove him to enter. Jibril, peace be upon him, came riding a female horse and went before Pharaoh's horse, and the people followed him until they were all completely in the sea, and it closed over them. The Children of Israel heard the water closing, and they had all come out of the sea, so they were amazed. Musa, peace be upon him, informed them that Pharaoh and his people had perished in it, so they asked for proof of this. The sea then cast up the bodies of the people, and Allah, exalted is He, placed Pharaoh upon a raised ground with his well-known coat of mail.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 80–82:

The Exalted said:

﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, and We made a appointment with you on the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quail.﴾ ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you. And whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed fallen.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward those who repent, believe, do righteousness, and then remain guided.﴾

The apparent meaning of these verses is that this speech was addressed to the Children of Israel at that time, when these blessings that God the Exalted enumerated for them arrived, and that between their exit from the sea and this statement there was a period and events. However, God the Exalted singles out for mention whatever He wills of that. It is also possible that this speech was addressed to the contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning: "This is what We did to your forebears." In that case, the Exalted One's words "Eat" would be understood as "It was said to them: Eat." The verse, on this reading, would be an interjection (i'tiraḍ) within the story of Musa (peace be upon him), its aim being to rebuke those present, since their predecessors did not persevere in rendering thanks for the blessings of God, blessed and exalted is He. The first meaning, however, is more apparent and clearer.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read: [anjaynā, wa-wāʿadnā, wa-nazzalnā ʿalaykum and razaqnākum]. However, Abu 'Amr read wa-ʿadnākum without an alif in the whole Qur'an. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: [anjaytu, wa-wāʿadtu, wa-nazzaltu and razaqnākum]. As for His saying "wa-wāʿadnākum" (we made an appointment with you), it was said that it is a dialect form of wa-ʿada, which does not require two agents.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

If it is taken in its customary sense, then the meeting, the covenant and the resolve upon that stand in place of an appointment (muwāʿada).

The narrative of this verse is that when God the Exalted delivered the Children of Israel and Pharaoh drowned, God, glorified and exalted is He, made a promise to the Children of Israel and Musa (peace be upon him) that they should proceed to the side of Mount Sinai, so that Musa might speak with Him there and converse with Him about what would be their welfare, through His commands and prohibitions. When they began to journey, Musa (peace be upon him) hastened to meet his Lord, as will be mentioned afterward.

One group said: this Tur is the one at which God the Exalted spoke with Musa first, when he saw the fire and was on his way from al-Sham to Egypt. Another group said: it is not that one. The word al-Tur means the mountain that has no trees (shuʿarāʾ) on it. As for His saying al-Ayman (the right), it may mean Yemen (al-Yaman), or it may mean "the right" (al-yamīn) in relation to "one who has a right side" (dhū yamīn), whether a human or other than a human. "Al-Manna wa-al-Salwā" was their food, and the complete explanation of both has already passed in al-Baqara.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ means the lawful and pleasant. This is because the meaning in this place includes both. People have differed about what is primarily intended by the word "good" (ṭayyib) in the Qur'an. Malik (may God have mercy on him) said: it means the lawful (ḥalāl). al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: it means what is agreeable to souls. This disagreement led to their jurisprudential discussion about insects and about the repugnant animals.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but do not transgress therein﴾ means: you go beyond the limit and act arbitrarily, as those did who acted in that way. The majority of people read: fa-yaḥilla with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, and yuḥallil with a kasra on the lām. al-Kisa'i alone read: fa-yaḥulla with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, and yaḥlul with a ḍamma on the lām. The meaning of the first is: then it becomes obligatory and due. The meaning of the second is: then it befalls and descends. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then he has indeed fallen﴾ means: he dropped from a height to a low place. From this is the saying of Khanafir:

*So he plunged down like the swoop of the eagle.*

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

Even if it is not a literal falling, it is a figurative comparison to one who falls. The literal meaning of falling is in the saying of another:

*…… the descent of the bucket which the rope has let go.*

The one who has fallen into a calamity or a predicament, after having been in safety from it, is compared to one who falls. So the verse is of this type; that is, he has fallen into Hell and into the wrath of God. It was also said that the verb is derived from al-Hawiya, which is the deepest part of Hell.

When God, blessed and exalted, warned against His wrath and against transgression in His blessings, He opened the door of hope for those who repent. Repentance (tawba) is an obligation upon all people, because of His saying in Surat al-Nur: ﴿And turn to God in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾ [al-Nur: 31] [al-Nur: 31]. People are of several grades in this matter. Either one is someone who has committed a sin while the capacity to repeat it remains; his repentance is remorse for what has passed and complete abstention from its like in the future. Or one is someone who committed a sin and then lost the capacity to do it, through old age or through an affliction; his repentance is remorse and the firm resolve to abandon it were he able. As for one who has not committed a sin, his repentance is the resolve to abandon every sin. Repentance from one sin is valid while one persists in another, and this is a restricted repentance. If the servant repents and then returns to the very same sin after a period, the skilled scholars of the Sunna (ḥudhdhāq ahl al-Sunna) may hold that God does not reinstate the first sin upon him, because the repentance was sincere (maḥḍa). It may also be held that He reinstates it, because it was a repentance he did not fulfil.

People have disputed about His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then remains guided﴾, in that they found guidance (hudā) to be included within faith and action. One group said: its meaning is: then he holds fast to Islam until he dies upon it. Another group said: its meaning is: he did not doubt his faith. Another group said: its meaning is: then he remained upright. Another group said: then he adhered to the Sunna of his Prophet (ﷺ). Another group said: its meaning is: then he hit upon the right deed. Another group said: its meaning is: then he came to know the matter of his old age. Another group said: its meaning is: and he befriended the People of the House.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

All of these are specifications of one of them to the exclusion of what is of its kind, which is far-fetched and not strong. What is strongest in the meaning of "then remains guided" is that it means: then he preserves his beliefs from opposing the truth in any matter. Guidance in this sense is other than faith and other than action, and many a believer who did righteous deeds has been ruined by his lack of guidance, such as the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), the Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on the status of the sinner), all the people of innovation (ahl al-bidaʿ, adherents of unwarranted novelties in religion), and the Kharijites. So the meaning of "then remains guided" is: then he walks upon a straight path in the beliefs of the Sharia. May God, the Exalted, make us among them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

In the preservation of beliefs, the greatness of the matter of the Sharia is contained.

The Exalted said:

﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, and We made a appointment with you on the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you the manna and the quail.﴾ ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, but do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you. And whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed fallen.﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward those who repent, believe, do righteousness, and then remain guided.﴾

The apparent meaning of these verses is that this speech was addressed to the Children of Israel at that time, when these blessings that God the Exalted enumerated for them arrived, and that between their exit from the sea and this statement there was a period and events. However, God the Exalted singles out for mention whatever He wills of that. It is also possible that this speech was addressed to the contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning: "This is what We did to your forebears." In that case, the Exalted One's words "Eat" would be understood as "It was said to them: Eat." The verse, on this reading, would be an interjection (i'tiraḍ) within the story of Musa (peace be upon him), its aim being to rebuke those present, since their predecessors did not persevere in rendering thanks for the blessings of God, blessed and exalted is He. The first meaning, however, is more apparent and clearer.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read: [anjaynā, wa-wāʿadnā, wa-nazzalnā ʿalaykum and razaqnākum]. However, Abu 'Amr read wa-ʿadnākum without an alif in the whole Qur'an. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: [anjaytu, wa-wāʿadtu, wa-nazzaltu and razaqnākum]. As for His saying "wa-wāʿadnākum" (we made an appointment with you), it was said that it is a dialect form of wa-ʿada, which does not require two agents.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

If it is taken in its customary sense, then the meeting, the covenant and the resolve upon that stand in place of an appointment (muwāʿada).

The narrative of this verse is that when God the Exalted delivered the Children of Israel and Pharaoh drowned, God, glorified and exalted is He, made a promise to the Children of Israel and Musa (peace be upon him) that they should proceed to the side of Mount Sinai, so that Musa might speak with Him there and converse with Him about what would be their welfare, through His commands and prohibitions. When they began to journey, Musa (peace be upon him) hastened to meet his Lord, as will be mentioned afterward.

One group said: this Tur is the one at which God the Exalted spoke with Musa first, when he saw the fire and was on his way from al-Sham to Egypt. Another group said: it is not that one. The word al-Tur means the mountain that has no trees (shuʿarāʾ) on it. As for His saying al-Ayman (the right), it may mean Yemen (al-Yaman), or it may mean "the right" (al-yamīn) in relation to "one who has a right side" (dhū yamīn), whether a human or other than a human. "Al-Manna wa-al-Salwā" was their food, and the complete explanation of both has already passed in al-Baqara.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ means the lawful and pleasant. This is because the meaning in this place includes both. People have differed about what is primarily intended by the word "good" (ṭayyib) in the Qur'an. Malik (may God have mercy on him) said: it means the lawful (ḥalāl). al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) said: it means what is agreeable to souls. This disagreement led to their jurisprudential discussion about insects and about the repugnant animals.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but do not transgress therein﴾ means: you go beyond the limit and act arbitrarily, as those did who acted in that way. The majority of people read: fa-yaḥilla with a kasra on the ḥāʾ, and yuḥallil with a kasra on the lām. al-Kisa'i alone read: fa-yaḥulla with a ḍamma on the ḥāʾ, and yaḥlul with a ḍamma on the lām. The meaning of the first is: then it becomes obligatory and due. The meaning of the second is: then it befalls and descends. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then he has indeed fallen﴾ means: he dropped from a height to a low place. From this is the saying of Khanafir:

*So he plunged down like the swoop of the eagle.*

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

Even if it is not a literal falling, it is a figurative comparison to one who falls. The literal meaning of falling is in the saying of another:

*…… the descent of the bucket which the rope has let go.*

The one who has fallen into a calamity or a predicament, after having been in safety from it, is compared to one who falls. So the verse is of this type; that is, he has fallen into Hell and into the wrath of God. It was also said that the verb is derived from al-Hawiya, which is the deepest part of Hell.

When God, blessed and exalted, warned against His wrath and against transgression in His blessings, He opened the door of hope for those who repent. Repentance (tawba) is an obligation upon all people, because of His saying in Surat al-Nur: ﴿And turn to God in repentance, all of you, O believers﴾ [al-Nur: 31] [al-Nur: 31]. People are of several grades in this matter. Either one is someone who has committed a sin while the capacity to repeat it remains; his repentance is remorse for what has passed and complete abstention from its like in the future. Or one is someone who committed a sin and then lost the capacity to do it, through old age or through an affliction; his repentance is remorse and the firm resolve to abandon it were he able. As for one who has not committed a sin, his repentance is the resolve to abandon every sin. Repentance from one sin is valid while one persists in another, and this is a restricted repentance. If the servant repents and then returns to the very same sin after a period, the skilled scholars of the Sunna (ḥudhdhāq ahl al-Sunna) may hold that God does not reinstate the first sin upon him, because the repentance was sincere (maḥḍa). It may also be held that He reinstates it, because it was a repentance he did not fulfil.

People have disputed about His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then remains guided﴾, in that they found guidance (hudā) to be included within faith and action. One group said: its meaning is: then he holds fast to Islam until he dies upon it. Another group said: its meaning is: he did not doubt his faith. Another group said: its meaning is: then he remained upright. Another group said: then he adhered to the Sunna of his Prophet (ﷺ). Another group said: its meaning is: then he hit upon the right deed. Another group said: its meaning is: then he came to know the matter of his old age. Another group said: its meaning is: and he befriended the People of the House.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

All of these are specifications of one of them to the exclusion of what is of its kind, which is far-fetched and not strong. What is strongest in the meaning of "then remains guided" is that it means: then he preserves his beliefs from opposing the truth in any matter. Guidance in this sense is other than faith and other than action, and many a believer who did righteous deeds has been ruined by his lack of guidance, such as the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination), the Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on the status of the sinner), all the people of innovation (ahl al-bidaʿ, adherents of unwarranted novelties in religion), and the Kharijites. So the meaning of "then remains guided" is: then he walks upon a straight path in the beliefs of the Sharia. May God, the Exalted, make us among them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

In the preservation of beliefs, the greatness of the matter of the Sharia is contained.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 83–86:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "They are right behind me on my path, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved.﴾

The narrative (qisas) of this verse is that when Musa (peace be upon him) set out with the Children of Israel toward the side of the Right Mount (al-Tur al-Ayman), where the appointment was that Allah would speak to Musa and bestow upon him that which would honour both the present and the hereafter, he saw, by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning), that he should go ahead alone, hastening toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, out of eagerness for nearness and longing for His intimate discourse. He appointed Harun (peace be upon him) as successor over the Children of Israel, and Musa (peace be upon him) said to them: "Proceed toward the side of the Mount." When Musa (peace be upon him) arrived and conversed with his Lord, He increased the term for him by ten (nights). At that point He made him stand before the meaning of his hastening without rising, so that Musa would inform Him that they were "on the trail," and the informing would reach Him concerning what they had done.

One group read "Ula'i" (أُولاءِ), and another group read "Ula'ay" (أولايَ) with a fatha on the ya'. His saying "ʿalā athārī" (عَلى أثَرِي) may be in the nominative position as a predicate after a predicate, and it may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). One group read "ʿalā athārī" (عَلى أثَرِي) with a fatha on the hamza and the thaʾ, and another group read "ʿalā ithrī" (عَلى إثْرِي) with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the thaʾ.

Musa (peace be upon him) informed Him that he had hastened only to seek His pleasure. Allah, the Exalted, informed him that He had tested the Children of Israel, meaning that He examined them through what al-Samiri had made. It may also be that He intends: "We cast them into fitnah," meaning into inclination toward desires and falling into discord. His saying "after you" (مِن بَعْدِكَ) means after your separation from them. One group read "wa-aḍallahumu al-Samiri" (وَأضَلَّهُمُ السامِرِيُّ) with the verb attributed to al-Samiri, and another group read "wa-aḍallu-humu al-Samiri" (وَأضَلُّهُمُ السامِرِيُّ) with a damma on the lam, as an inchoative and predicate, stating about al-Samiri that he was the most misguided of the people.

"Al-Samiri" (السامِرِيُّ) was a man from the Children of Israel. It is said that he was the maternal cousin of Musa (peace be upon him). Another group said he was not from the Children of Israel, but that his origin was from the non-Arabs (ʿajam), from the people of Kerman; the first view is more sound. The account of al-Samiri is that he was a hypocrite, possessing tricks and sorcery, and he took a handful (qabḍa) from the trace of Jibril (peace be upon him). He knew that by what Allah had empowered him with for the trial of the people, he could accomplish with that handful what he willed of what is permissible for Allah, the Exalted; for if he had claimed prophethood with that calf, it would not have been valid, nor would it have been possible for it to low, nor for the trick to be completed in it. But when he claimed for it lordship (ruboobiyya), while the signs of his lie were manifest and clear, the trial through him was valid and that was permissible for Allah, the Exalted, like the story of the Dajjal, to whom customs are broken because he claims lordship; and had he been a claimant to prophethood, none of that would have been valid. So when al-Samiri saw that Musa had gone away, and saw the rest of the Children of Israel, in their seeking from Musa gods when they passed by a people worshipping idols in the form of cows (and it is said: they were actual cows), he knew that he would tempt them by this path. It is related that he said to them: "The jewelry you have from the property of the Copts is an ugly thing for you to keep; but gather it with me until Allah judges for you concerning it." It is also said that Harun (peace be upon him) commanded them to gather it and place it in a pit until Musa comes and seeks permission from his Lord concerning it. It is also said: rather, the wealth they gathered for al-Samiri was from what the sea had cast up of the wealth of the Copts who drowned with Pharaoh. It is related—despite this disagreement—that the jewelry was gathered before al-Samiri, and that he fashioned the calf and cast the handful into it, and it lowed. It is also related—and this is the more sound and the more common view—that the people cast the jewelry into a pit or the like, and he cast the handful upon it, and the calf took bodily form. This is the aspect of Allah's trial of them. On this view we say: a customary law was broken for al-Samiri; but as for his fashioning it, no custom was broken for him, and they were tried then only by its lowing alone, and that sound may be produced in bodies through craft. When Allah informed Musa (peace be upon him) of what had occurred, Musa returned to his people angry and grieved over them, from the standpoint that he had the power to change their wrong.

His saying "asifan" (أسِفًا) means grieved, sorrowful, since he knew it was a place of punishment which he had to avert, and it was inevitable. In the speech of the Arabs, "al-asaf" (الأسَفُ), when it comes from one who has power over one below him, is anger, and when it comes from one lower toward one stronger, it is grief. Reflect on this, for it is consistent, if Allah wills.

He knew that by what Allah had empowered him with for the trial of the people, he could accomplish with that handful what he willed of what is permissible for Allah, the Exalted; for if he had claimed prophethood with that calf, it would not have been valid, nor would it have been possible for it to low, nor for the trick to be completed in it. But when he claimed for it lordship (ruboobiyya), while the signs of his lie were manifest and clear, the trial through him was valid and that was permissible for Allah, the Exalted, like the story of the Dajjal, to whom customs are broken because he claims lordship; and had he been a claimant to prophethood, none of that would have been valid. So when al-Samiri saw that Musa had gone away, and saw the rest of the Children of Israel, in their seeking from Musa gods when they passed by a people worshipping idols in the form of cows (and it is said: they were actual cows), he knew that he would tempt them by this path. It is related that he said to them: "The jewelry you have from the property of the Copts is an ugly thing for you to keep; but gather it with me until Allah judges for you concerning it." It is also said that Harun (peace be upon him) commanded them to gather it and place it in a pit until Musa comes and seeks permission from his Lord concerning it. It is also said: rather, the wealth they gathered for al-Samiri was from what the sea had cast up of the wealth of the Copts who drowned with Pharaoh. It is related—despite this disagreement—that the jewelry was gathered before al-Samiri, and that he fashioned the calf and cast the handful into it, and it lowed. It is also related—and this is the more sound and the more common view—that the people cast the jewelry into a pit or the like, and he cast the handful upon it, and the calf took bodily form. This is the aspect of Allah's trial of them. On this view we say: a customary law was broken for al-Samiri; but as for his fashioning it, no custom was broken for him, and they were tried then only by its lowing alone, and that sound may be produced in bodies through craft. When Allah informed Musa (peace be upon him) of what had occurred, Musa returned to his people angry and grieved over them, from the standpoint that he had the power to change their wrong.

His saying "asifan" (أسِفًا) means grieved, sorrowful, since he knew it was a place of punishment which he had to avert, and it was inevitable. In the speech of the Arabs, "al-asaf" (الأسَفُ), when it comes from one who has power over one below him, is anger, and when it comes from one lower toward one stronger, it is grief. Reflect on this, for it is consistent, if Allah wills.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 87–88:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said: "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Has the time seemed long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your appointment with me?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86] ﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power, but we were laden with burdens of the people's ornaments, so we threw them, and thus did al-Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing sound.﴾

Musa (peace be upon him) reproached his people with this statement. The "good promise" is what He had promised them of reaching the side of the right slope of the Mount (al-Tur), and what followed of conquests in the land, and forgiveness for whoever repents and believes, and other things that Allah the Exalted promised to the people of His obedience. As for His saying "a promise" (wa'dan), it may be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), with the second object implied; or it may mean "the promised thing" (al-mawud), in which case it is itself the second object.

Then he confronted them with excuses that did not exist and could not be valid for them: the length of the period, so that a breach in the appointment would become apparent to them, and the desire for Allah's wrath. None of that had occurred, but they acted like those who had no religion. The punishment was called "wrath" because it arises from wrath. And wrath, if taken to mean will, is an attribute of essence; if taken to mean the manifestation of vengeance and punishment, it is an attribute of action. So it lies between the two states.

Nafi' and 'Asim read "bi-malkina" with a fatha on the mim; Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-mulkina" with a damma; Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "bi-milkina" with a kasra. Abu 'Ali said: these are dialectal variants.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the speech is that they have one meaning, but Abu 'Ali and others have distinguished between their meanings. As for the damma on the mim, its meaning according to Abu 'Ali is: "We had no king so that we would break your appointment by his power and authority; rather we broke it by an opinion which led to what al-Samiri did. The meaning is not that they had a king." It is like the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"He complains of a fall from her, though the wastelands have made her dance until her back became humped."

That is, there is no fall from her so that she complains. He said: this is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not beg of people at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], that is, there is no begging from them so that there would be importunity from them.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this in these examples is not certain from Abu 'Ali's statement; he merely followed the view of al-Zajjaj without critique. I have explained this meaning in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not beg of people at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 273], and it became clear that this verse is not like these examples, because they did not remove the disagreement, whereas in the examples both possibilities are affirmed.

As for the fatha on the mim, it is a verbal noun from malaka, and the meaning is: we did not do that because we possessed the right course and were not granted success in it; rather our own souls overcame us.

As for the kasra on the mim, its use is frequent for what the hand possesses, but it is used for matters that a person firmly determines, and its meaning is like the meaning of the previous one. The verbal noun is in both cases annexed to the agent, and the object is implied, meaning: by our determination of the right course. This is like how it is sometimes annexed to the object while the agent is implied, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿by your asking of his ewe to his ewes﴾ [Sad: 24], and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from supplication for good﴾ [Fussilat: 49].

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read "hummilna" with a damma on the ha' and a shadda on the mim; Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "hamalna" with a fatha on the ha' and the mim. "Al-awzar" means the burdens, and this naming may be because they are heavy in body, or it may be because they incurred sin in casting them and it became clear to them that this was the truth, so they were sins for whoever carried them. His saying, "So thus did al-Samiri cast," means: just as we cast, so likewise al-Samiri cast what was in his hand.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These expressions imply that al-Samiri did not fashion the calf.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed about the act of al-Samiri by His saying: ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body﴾, and the meaning of "a body" (jasadan) is a figure without a spirit in it. It was also said that the meaning of "jasadan" is: it does not feed. And "al-khuwar" is the lowing of a cow. A group said: this calf used to low and walk.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Thus the trial comes from Allah, the Exalted; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Another group said: its lowing was only by the wind, which entered from its rear and exited from its mouth, so it made a sound because of that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 89–91:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿So they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88] ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word, and that it possesses for them no harm and no benefit?﴾ ﴿And Harun had already said to them before this, "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."﴾ ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us."﴾

The pronoun in His saying "So they said" refers to the Children of Israel, meaning: they went astray when their elders said to their young, and "this" is a reference to the calf. His Exalted saying "but he forgot" may be part of the speech of the Children of Israel, meaning: Musa, peace be upon him, forgot his Lord and his God and went seeking Him in other than its place. It may also be that "but he forgot" is a report from God Most High about the Samiri, that he forgot his religion and the path of truth.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So forgetting in the first interpretation means heedlessness, and in the second it means abandonment.

Then God Most High juxtaposed their address with His saying "Do they not see," meaning: Have those who went astray not become clear that this calf is merely an inanimate body that does not speak, does not return a word, and neither harms nor benefits? These are attributes with which the createdness and incapacity cannot remain hidden, because if these attributes were present in it, they would necessitate its being a god. One group read "allā yarji'u" with a raised ʿayn (ya'ruju/yarjiʿu as yarji'u with the damma), and "wa-anna," on this reading, is the light form of the heavy, and the estimate is: "annahu lā yarji'u." Another group read "allā yarji'a," and "wa-anna," on this reading, is the governing particle.

God, Mighty and Majestic, informed that Harun, peace be upon him, had said to them at the very beginning of the calf's affair: it is only a trial, a affliction and a deception from the Samiri, and "your Lord is the Most Merciful," the One who possesses power, knowledge, creation and origination, "so follow me" to the mountain to which God Most High promised you, "and obey my command" in what I have mentioned to you. One group read "innamā" and "wa-inna rabbakumu al-Raḥmāna" with the two hamzas kasra'd. One group read "annamā" and "wa-anna" with the hamza fatha'd. One group read "innamā" with kasra and "anna" with fatha, and the middle reading is weak.

The Children of Israel said, when Harun, peace be upon him, admonished them and urged them toward the truth: "We will not cease to be worshippers of this god, devoted to it," meaning: constant in it. And "al-ʿukūf" is bending over a thing from the intensity of constant attachment to it, and from it is the saying of the rajaz poet:

؎ ʿakafa al-Nabīṭu yalʿabūna al-Fanzajā

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 92–94:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, ﴾ ﴿from following me? Did you then disobey my order?" ﴾ ﴿He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾

In the narration of the story there is an ellipsis (iqtiḍāb) indicated by what has been mentioned. Its implied meaning is: Musa, peace be upon him, returned and found the matter as Allah, exalted is He, had told him, so he began to rebuke Harun with this statement.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "ألّا تَتَّبِعَنِ" (allā tattabi‘anī) with the ya' omitted. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' affirmed in connection (wasl), and Ibn Kathir pauses with the ya', while Abu 'Amr pauses without the ya'.

His saying "allā tattabi‘anī" may mean: "from following me with the Children of Israel toward Mount Tur." In that case, Harun's excuse, peace be upon him, carries the sense: "Had I done that, a group would have walked with me while another group remained upon the worship of the calf, so the gathering would have scattered, and I feared your blame for causing division."

It may also mean: "not to proceed with my course and my method of reform and rectification." In that case, Harun's excuse, peace be upon him, carries the sense: "The matter had grown severe, and had I strengthened myself against them, fighting and discord of word would have occurred, which would have been division among the Children of Israel. I only refrained because I exerted my utmost effort."

His, may He be exalted, saying "allā tattabi‘anī" means: "What prevented you from following me?" Scholars differed regarding the function of "lā" here. One group said it is superfluous (zā’ida). The skilled grammarians (ḥudhdhāq al-nuḥāh) held that it is emphatic (mu’akkida), and that the speech contains an implied verb, as if he said: "What prevented you from that, or singled you out for that, or something similar, [namely] 'allā tattabi‘anī'?" What precedes and follows indicates this and requires it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Hafs from 'Asim read "يابْنَ أُمْ" (yā ibna umm), which may mean "yā ibna ummā," with the alif dropped for lightness, or may treat the two words as a single name, built like khamsata 'ashar. Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "يا بْنَ أُمْ" with the kasra, by dropping the ya' for lightness; this is anomalous (shādhdh), because it is not like the ya' in your saying "yā ghulāmī," but rather like the ya' in your saying "yā ghulāma ghulāmī," and this is a ya' that is not dropped. It may also be that the two words are treated as one name, then he added it to himself and dropped the ya', as is dropped from singular nouns when they are made into an idafa, as in "yā ghulāmu." One group said: Harun was not the brother of Musa, peace be upon him, except through his mother.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Another group said: He was his full brother, and he called him by their mother because calling by the mother is more tender and more compelling of compassion. Musa, peace be upon him, seized Harun's beard in anger, and he was of a sharp temper, peace be upon him.

Did you then disobey my order?" ﴾ ﴿He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾

In the narration of the story there is an ellipsis (iqtiḍāb) indicated by what has been mentioned. Its implied meaning is: Musa, peace be upon him, returned and found the matter as Allah, exalted is He, had told him, so he began to rebuke Harun with this statement.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "ألّا تَتَّبِعَنِ" (allā tattabi‘anī) with the ya' omitted. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya' affirmed in connection (wasl), and Ibn Kathir pauses with the ya', while Abu 'Amr pauses without the ya'.

His saying "allā tattabi‘anī" may mean: "from following me with the Children of Israel toward Mount Tur." In that case, Harun's excuse, peace be upon him, carries the sense: "Had I done that, a group would have walked with me while another group remained upon the worship of the calf, so the gathering would have scattered, and I feared your blame for causing division."

It may also mean: "not to proceed with my course and my method of reform and rectification." In that case, Harun's excuse, peace be upon him, carries the sense: "The matter had grown severe, and had I strengthened myself against them, fighting and discord of word would have occurred, which would have been division among the Children of Israel. I only refrained because I exerted my utmost effort."

His, may He be exalted, saying "allā tattabi‘anī" means: "What prevented you from following me?" Scholars differed regarding the function of "lā" here. One group said it is superfluous (zā’ida). The skilled grammarians (ḥudhdhāq al-nuḥāh) held that it is emphatic (mu’akkida), and that the speech contains an implied verb, as if he said: "What prevented you from that, or singled you out for that, or something similar, [namely] 'allā tattabi‘anī'?" As for "al-Samiri", it is said that he is attributed to a tribe of the Children of Israel, and it is also said that he is attributed to a village called Samira.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is known today in the land of Egypt. It is also said that his name was Musa ibn Zafar.

Another group read "basirtu" with a kasrah on the ṣād. It may be from al-basirah (insight), and it may be from al-basar (sight), because in the matter of the Samiri there was something beyond what people perceived by sight, namely the face of Jibril, peace be upon him, and his horse, and by insight, namely what he knew: that if he threw the handful together with the ornaments, what he wanted would come to him from that. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "tubsirū" with the tā' from above, meaning Musa, peace be upon him, together with the Children of Israel.

Al-Hasan, in one of the reports from him, read "qubḍatan" with a ḍammah on the qāf. "Al-Rasul" is Jibril, peace be upon him, and "al-athar" is the dust beneath the hoof of his horse.

This is weak.

Its use in this manner is frequent. Abu ʿUbaydah and others compared it to nizāl and darāk and the like, and the comparison is sound in respect of being transferred forms, but it differs from them in that these are transferred from the imperative, whereas "misās" and "fujjār" are transferred from the verbal noun. Tamim is like the people of the Samiri.

And his saying:

Ala, no, the Samiri does not desire contact (misās).

The majority read "tukhlafahu" with a fatḥah on the lām, meaning: no failure will occur in it. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "lan tukhlifahu" with a kasrah on the lām, meaning: you will not be able to evade it or deviate from it, and so you will not escape the appointment of the punishment. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "lan nukhlifahu" with a nūn. Abu al-Fath said: the meaning is: we will not find it left behind.

All of them carry the meaning of threat and warning.

Except that the noble camels among the mounts do not sense it (aḥussna bihi), so they are averse to it.

Such a one has become like the Samiri, when Musa said to him: "No contact" (lā misāsan).

From it also is the saying of Ru'bah:

Until the Azd say "No contact" (lā misāsan).

Its use in this manner is frequent. Abu Haywah read "lā masāsi" with a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the sīn, (p-129) and it is a form transferred (ma'dūl) from the verbal noun, like fujjār and the like. Abu ʿUbaydah and others compared it to nizāl and darāk and the like, and the comparison is sound in respect of being transferred forms, but it differs from them in that these are transferred from the imperative, whereas "misās" and "fujjār" are transferred from the verbal noun. From this is the saying of the poet:

Tamim is like the people of the Samiri.

And his saying:

Ala, no, the Samiri does not desire contact (misās).

The majority read "tukhlafahu" with a fatḥah on the lām, meaning: no failure will occur in it. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "lan tukhlifahu" with a kasrah on the lām, meaning: you will not be able to evade it or deviate from it, and so you will not escape the appointment of the punishment. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "lan nukhlifahu" with a nūn. Abu al-Fath said: the meaning is: we will not find it left behind.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of them carry the meaning of threat and warning.

Then he rebuked him, peace be upon him, with his saying: ﴿And look at your god﴾ and the verse, that is: look at your handiwork and our alteration of it, and our returning the matter concerning it to what is obligatory. A group read "ẓalta" with a fatḥah on the ẓā', by omitting one lām, and a group read "ẓilta" with a kasrah on the ẓā', by transferring the vowel of the lām to the ẓā' and then omitting it afterwards, like the saying of the poet:

Except that the noble camels among the mounts do not sense it (aḥussna bihi), so they are averse to it.

(p-130) He meant: aḥsusna, so the vowel of the sīn was transferred to the ḥā' and then it was omitted for lightness; and in some reports: ḥusayna. A group read "ẓallita", and "ẓalla" means: he remained doing a thing by day, but it may also be used of one who persists day and night, in the sense of ṭafiqa. "ʿĀkifan" means: remaining constantly.

A group read "lanuḥriqannahu" with a lightened rāʾ, meaning: with fire. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them, read "lanaḥrujannahu" with a fatḥah on the nūn and a ḍammah on the rāʾ, lightened, meaning: we will file it with a file. Nafi' and others read "lanuḥarriqannahu" with a ḍammah on the nūn and a kasrah on the rāʾ with shaddah; this is intensive doubling of intensity, not transitivity, and this reading admits of burning with fire and admits of filing with a file. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with them both: "lanadhbahannahu thumma lanuḥriqannahu thumma lananfakhannahu" (we will surely slaughter it, then we will surely burn it, then we will surely scatter it). This reading, together with the report of those who narrated that the calf became flesh and blood, implies that there was burning with fire; otherwise, if it was a lifeless mass of gold, then it was burning by filing, unless it was melting, and the scattering would be used figuratively for its dispersal in the sea in molten form. A group read "lanansifannahu" with a kasrah on the sīn, and a group read "lanansufannahu" with a ḍammah on the sīn. "Al-nasf" is the wind's scattering of dust, and whatever is like it, such as the sifting of a sieve and the like, is nasf. "Al-yamm" is water that covers, from a sea or a river, and whatever water covers a person is yamm. "Nasfan" is an emphatic verbal noun, and the lām in his saying "lanuḥarriqannahu" is the lām of oath.

Among the narratives in this verse is that Musa, peace be upon him, pulverized the calf until he reduced it to something like dust, then scattered it into the sea, then commanded the Children of Israel that all of them drink from the water; whoever among them had love of the calf in his heart, the gold would come out on his lip as a disgrace to him. Makki, may Allah have mercy on him, said, and he attributed it (p-131): that Musa, peace be upon him, was with the seventy at the time of the private conversation, and at that moment the matter of the calf occurred; and that Allah, blessed and exalted, informed Musa of that, so he concealed it from them and brought them until he heard the clamour of the Children of Israel around the calf, and then Musa informed them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the report of the majority, contrary to it. Rather, Musa alone hastened ahead, and the matter of the calf occurred; then Musa, peace be upon him, came and did to the calf what he did; then after that he went out with the seventy in the sense of intercession for the sin of the Children of Israel, and so that he would also inform them of the matter of the private conversation. So Musa, peace be upon him, had two setouts. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verse 98–102:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no god; He encompasses all things in knowledge.﴾ ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has preceded, and We have certainly given you from Us a reminder.﴾ ﴿Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein eternally, and evil will it be for them as a load on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed.﴾

This is an address from Musa (peace be upon him) to all of the Children of Israel, clarifying for them. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿wasi'a kulla shay'in 'ilman﴾ means: His knowledge encompassed everything. "'Ilman" is a tamyiz (specification of comparison/accusative of specification). This is like their saying: "tafaqa'at shahman" (it burst, [as to] fat) and "tasabbabat 'arqan" (it poured, [as to] sweat). The verbal noun is originally the subject (fa'il), but the verb is attributed to something else and the verbal noun is put in the accusative as a tamyiz. Mujahid and Qatada read: "wassa'a kulla shay'in" with the sin fathah and shaddah, meaning: He created things and multiplied them by innovation, so He made them existent, extending them.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some of the news of what has preceded﴾ is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: just as We related to you this account of the Children of Israel in the story of the calf, thus do We relate to you. It is as if He said: "Thus do We relate to you," so this is an enumeration of His blessing. His saying: "what has preceded" intends what has preceded the period of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Al-dhikr" is the Qur'an. One group read "yahmilu" with a kasrah on the mim, and another group read "yuhammalu" with a fathah on the mim and shaddah. His saying: ﴿whoever turns away from it﴾ means: by disbelieving in it and denying it. "Al-wizr" is the heaviness, and here it is the heaviness of punishment, as evidenced by His saying: "abiding therein eternally." "Hilman" is a tamyiz, "yawma" is an adverbial of time, and the second "yawma" is a substitute (badal) for it. The majority read "yunfakhu" with a dammah on the ya' and the verb in the passive voice. One group read "yanfukhu" with a fathah on the ya' and the verb in the active voice, meaning the angel blows. Abu 'Amr alone read "nanfukhu" with the nun, meaning by Our command and Our permission, and this reading (p-132) suits His saying "nahshuru." The majority read "fi al-sur" with a sukun on the waw, and the position of the majority is that it is the horn into which Israfil blows, and the hadiths have come with this. One group said: "al-suwar" is the plural of "surah," like "tamrah" and "tamr." 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read "fi al-suwari" with a fathah on the waw, and this is explicit in the resurrection of bodies from graves. One group, which is the majority, read "wa-nahshuru" with the nun; another group read "wa-yahshuru" with the ya'; and another group read "wa-yuhsharu" with a dammah on the ya', "al-mujrimuna" as the object of a verb whose subject is not named, and this is a reading that differs from the script of the Mushaf.

As for His saying: "zurqan," people differed about its meaning. One group said: on their being gathered at the beginning of their standing, with black complexions and blue eyes, so this is a kind of disfigurement, and then after that they will be made blind; and these are stages. Another group said: they will be gathered thirsty, and intense thirst returns the blackness of the eye to whiteness, so it is as if the blackness of their eyes turns white from the intensity of thirst. Another group said: he meant blue complexions, and this is an extreme of disfigurement, because they come with the colour of ash. The most common usage of the Arabic language is to call this colour "azraq" (blue), and from it comes the blueness of water. The poet said:

﴿When they reached the water, its watering-places blue, they set down the staves of the settled encampment.﴾

And from it their saying: "a blue spear-head," because it is similar to that colour.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 108–111:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿On that Day they will follow the Caller, with no deviance from Him; and voices will be hushed before the All-Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a faint whisper.﴾ ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the All-Merciful has permitted and with whose word He is pleased.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they cannot encompass Him in knowledge.﴾ ﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting. And he will have failed who bears injustice.﴾

The meaning: On the Day when We blow away the mountains, the creatures will follow the Caller of Allah, the Exalted, to the place of gathering (al-mahshar). This is similar to His saying: ﴿Hastening toward the Caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. His saying ﴿with no deviance from Him﴾ may mean that it is a report about Him, i.e., there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also mean that no one can turn away from following Him and walking toward His voice. "Khushu'" (humility) means submission and lowliness; with regard to voices it is a metaphor for concealment and being hidden. The meaning of "before the All-Merciful" is due to His awe and the terror of the manifestation of His power. "Al-Hams" is a faint, low, muted sound. It may be that by "the audible whisper" is meant their murmuring among themselves and their secret speech, and it may be that it means the sound of footsteps, while the sounds of speech are silent.

As for "man" in His saying ﴿except for one whom the All-Merciful has permitted﴾, the exception may be connected (muttasil), and "man" is in the accusative position, referring to the one for whom intercession is made, so the meaning is: except for one for whom the All-Merciful has permitted intercession. It may also be disconnected (munqati'), on the assumption: "But the one whom the All-Merciful has permitted will intercede." Then "man" is in the accusative position by way of exception, and it may also be in the nominative position, just as both possibilities are allowed in your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey, and except a donkey." The accusative is more eloquent. "Man," according to these interpretations, refers to the intercessor, and it may also refer to the one for whom intercession is made.

As for His saying ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, one group said: it means the angels; another group said: it means all of His creation. The discussion of the order of "before" and "behind" has already been presented in more than one place. Moreover, a group of exegetes said regarding this verse: "what is behind them" is the world (al-dunya), and "what is before them" is the matter of the Hereafter, the reward and the punishment. This applies if He presents them in a state of standing until He makes them like bodies; but if we consider them in the sequence of time, the matter is the reverse, according to the ruling we explained earlier.

As for His saying ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾, its meaning is: they will be abased. "Al-'ani" is the captive, and from it comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding women: "They are 'awan (captives) with you." This is the state of people on the Day of Resurrection. Talq ibn Habib said: Allah, the Exalted, intended the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If it has been narrated that people will be prostrating on the Day of Resurrection, and this verse is taken as a report, then his saying is sound. But if he meant the prostration of this world, then he has corrupted the meaning. "Al-Qayyum" is an intensive form derived from His standing over every thing in what is due to it, may He be Mighty and Majestic. "Khaba" means: he did not succeed and did not attain what he sought. "Injustice" (al-zulm) encompasses both polytheism and sins, and the failure of every bearer is in proportion to the injustice he carried: the failure of the polytheist is absolute, while the failure of the sinner is restricted to a time and a limit in punishment.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿Hastening toward the Caller﴾ [al-Qamar: 8]. His saying ﴿with no deviance from Him﴾ may mean that it is a report about Him, i.e., there is no doubt about it, and its existence does not contradict its report. It may also mean that no one can turn away from following Him and walking toward His voice. "Khushu'" (humility) means submission and lowliness; with regard to voices it is a metaphor for concealment and being hidden. The meaning of "before the All-Merciful" is due to His awe and the terror of the manifestation of His power. "Al-Hams" is a faint, low, muted sound. It may be that by "the audible whisper" is meant their murmuring among themselves and their secret speech, and it may be that it means the sound of footsteps, while the sounds of speech are silent.

As for "man" in His saying ﴿except for one whom the All-Merciful has permitted﴾, the exception may be connected (muttasil), and "man" is in the accusative position, referring to the one for whom intercession is made, so the meaning is: except for one for whom the All-Merciful has permitted intercession. It may also be disconnected (munqati'), on the assumption: "But the one whom the All-Merciful has permitted will intercede." Then "man" is in the accusative position by way of exception, and it may also be in the nominative position, just as both possibilities are allowed in your saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey, and except a donkey." The accusative is more eloquent. "Man," according to these interpretations, refers to the intercessor, and it may also refer to the one for whom intercession is made.

As for His saying ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, one group said: it means the angels; another group said: it means all of His creation. The discussion of the order of "before" and "behind" has already been presented in more than one place. Moreover, a group of exegetes said regarding this verse: "what is behind them" is the world (al-dunya), and "what is before them" is the matter of the Hereafter, the reward and the punishment. This applies if He presents them in a state of standing until He makes them like bodies; but if we consider them in the sequence of time, the matter is the reverse, according to the ruling we explained earlier.

As for His saying ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾, its meaning is: they will be abased. "Al-'ani" is the captive, and from it comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ regarding women: "They are 'awan (captives) with you." This is the state of people on the Day of Resurrection. Talq ibn Habib said: Allah, the Exalted, intended the prostration of people upon their faces and the seven limbs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If it has been narrated that people will be prostrating on the Day of Resurrection, and this verse is taken as a report, then his saying is sound. But if he meant the prostration of this world, then he has corrupted the meaning. "Al-Qayyum" is an intensive form derived from His standing over every thing in what is due to it, may He be Mighty and Majestic. "Khaba" means: he did not succeed and did not attain what he sought. "Injustice" (al-zulm) encompasses both polytheism and sins, and the failure of every bearer is in proportion to the injustice he carried: the failure of the polytheist is absolute, while the failure of the sinner is restricted to a time and a limit in punishment.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 112–114:**

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer will fear neither injustice nor diminution.﴾ ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have varied in it some of the warnings, that perhaps they may fear God, or that it may renew for them a remembrance.﴾ ﴿So exalted is God, the King, the Truth. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾

His words, "Whoever does" (man ya'mal), are parallel to His words, "Whoever carries injustice" (man hamala zulman) [Ta-Ha: 111]. In His words, "of the righteous deeds" (min al-salihat), there is facilitation in the Law, because the "min" is the partitive "min" (min al-tab'id). "Injustice" (al-zulm) is more general than "diminution" (al-hadm), and the two are close in meaning and overlap. However, given how they are paired in this verse, some people went on to restrict each one to a specific meaning. They said: "Injustice" is that his evil deeds are magnified upon him and multiply beyond what is due, and "diminution" is that his good deeds are undone and reduced. All of them read "fa-la yakhaf" (then he will not fear) as a statement, except Ibn Kathir, who read "fa-la yakhaf" as a prohibition (nahy).

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We have sent it down﴾, meaning: just as We decreed these matters and made them a matter of watchfulness for the servants, so too We have warned these people of Our command. We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an and We threatened in it with kinds of warnings, so that perhaps they—according to human expectation and hope—will fear God, dread His punishment, and thereby believe and remember His blessings upon them and what He warned them of of His painful punishment. This is the interpretation of one group regarding His words, ﴿or that it may renew for them a remembrance﴾. Another group said its meaning is: or that it may bring them honor and preserve their faith and a good remembrance among those who came before. Al-Hasan al-Basri read "aw yahduth" with the thа' (ث) unvocalized (sakinah), and Mujahid read "aw nuhdith" with the nun and the thа' unvocalized. There is no justification for the jazm (apocopate) reading except that the letter carrying the case (harf al-i'rab, the final letter that marks grammatical case) is unvocalized because of the difficulty of its vowel (istithqal), and this is like the line of Jarir:

﴿............................ and the Arabs do not know you﴾

His words, ﴿So exalted is God, the King, the Truth﴾, are a conclusion to the discourse, because when He had mentioned the attribute of His sovereignty on the Day of Resurrection, the greatness of His power, the humility of His servants, and His gentleness toward them, He concluded that with this expression, and after that He made the command in another kind of speech. His words, ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾, a group said: its cause is that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to fear, during the time when Jibril (peace be upon him) was speaking to him, that he would forget the beginning of the Qur'an, so he would recite before Jibril (peace be upon him) had finished the revelation. So this was revealed about that, and it has the same meaning as His words: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16]. Another group said: the cause of this verse is that when the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), he would order it written down immediately. So God, the Exalted, commanded in this verse that he be patient until its meanings are explained to him and established for him. Another group said: the cause of the verse is that "a woman complained to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that her husband had slapped her, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her: 'Retaliation (qisas) is between you two.' Then ﴿Men are the protectors of women﴾ [al-Nisa: 34] was revealed." This verse came with the meaning of making certain of the ruling by the Qur'an until it is clarified. And God knows best.

The majority read "min qabli an yaqdiya ilayka wahyahu" (before its revelation is completed to you), and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read "min qabli an yaqdiya ilayka wahyahu" likewise. The rest of the verse is clear, in desire for what is good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 115–117:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, lest you suffer.﴾

Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning is: and if these disbelievers, O Muhammad, turn away from My signs, oppose My messengers, and obey Iblis, then their father Adam did this long ago.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is weak, because making Adam an example for the disbelieving deniers is nothing of substance, and Adam only disobeyed through an interpretation (ta'wil), so in this there is a disparagement of him (ﷺ). As for the apparent meaning of this verse, it is either the beginning of a narrative that has no connection to what precedes it, or its connection is taken to be that when Muhammad (ﷺ) was charged not to hasten with the Qur'an, he was given an example from a prophet before him who was charged and then forgot and was punished, so that it would be stronger in warning and more emphatic in the covenant with Muhammad (ﷺ). The word "covenant" (ahd) here means injunction (wasiyya), and "forgot" (nasiya) means "left" (taraka); forgetfulness in the sense of heedlessness is not possible here, since no punishment attaches to one who forgets. Al-A'mash read "fa-nasiya" with a sukun on the ya', and its basis is the seeking of lightness. And "resolve" (azm) is persistence upon a belief in whatever matter it may be. Adam, peace be upon him, held the belief that he would not eat from the tree, but when Iblis whispered to him he did not hold firm (lam ya'zim) upon his belief. (p-138) Some exegetes expressed "resolve" here as patience, as preservation, and other things that are more general than the true meaning of resolve. What was covenanted to Adam, peace be upon him, was that he not approach the tree, and he was also informed that Iblis was an enemy to him. Abu Umama, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the dreams of the children of Adam were gathered from the time Allah created creation until the Day of Resurrection and placed in one pan of a balance, and the dream of Adam, peace be upon him, were placed in the other pan, it would outweigh them. And the Most High has said: ﴿and We found in him no resolve.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"⦆ — the verse is the beginning of a narrative, and the governing element of "when" (idh) is an implied verb. This story has already been fully covered, but we mention from it what the wording of this verse requires. As for the angels, it is said that all of them were commanded to do this, and it is said: rather a noble group of them, whose number was twenty-two. The "prostration" they were commanded to perform was a prostration of honour to Adam, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, and an act of worship to Allah the Most High. His saying: ﴿except Iblis﴾ — the exception is connected according to the view of the one who considers Iblis to be among the angels, and disconnected according to the view of the one who says he is of a different kind than the angels, called the jinn. His saying: ﴿So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, lest you suffer﴾ means: let there not occur from you both obedience to him in his seduction, for that would be the cause of your expulsion from the Garden. Then He singled out Adam, peace be upon him, with His saying "lest you suffer," since he was the first addressed and the principal intended in the speech. It is said: rather, this is because Allah the Most High placed hardship in the livelihood of this world in the domain of men. It is narrated that when Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down, a red ox descended with him, and he would plough and wipe the sweat; this is the hardship from which he was warned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 118–121:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:
