**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 20, verses 122–126:**

The Exalted and Majestic has said:

﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾ ﴿He said: "Go down from it, all of you, some of you enemies to others. Then, when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be wretched."﴾ ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance, for him is a straitened life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ ﴿He will say: "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was able to see?"﴾ ﴿He will say: "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; likewise today you are forgotten."﴾

"Ijtabāhu" means: He chose him and selected him. "Tāba ʿalayhi" means: He returned him from a state of disobedience to a state of regret, and guided him to the rectitude of his words and deeds. He also carried out His punishment, the Exalted and Majestic, by making him descend from the Garden.

His saying, exalted is He, "Ihbiṭā" ("Go down"), is addressed to Adam and Ḥawwāʾ (Eve). Then, by His saying "jamīʿan" ("all of you"), He informed them that Iblīs and the serpent would descend with them, and that enmity would exist between them and their descendants until the Day of Resurrection. "ʿAduww" (enemy) is applied to the singular, the dual, and the plural. His saying, exalted is He, "Fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum" ("Then, when there comes to you") is a conditional clause, and its response is in His saying "Faman ittabaʿa hudāya" ("whoever follows My guidance") and what follows it up to the end of the second division. "Al-Hudā" (guidance) means the call of the sharʿ (revealed law). Then He informed them that whoever follows His guidance and believes in it will neither go astray in this world nor be wretched in the Hereafter, and that whoever turns away from the remembrance of God and disbelieves in Him, for him is a straitened life. "Al-Ḍank" (straitened) means harsh, difficult hardship of life, whether in dwellings or in the places of war and the like. From it is the saying of ʿAntara:

"… and if they alight on a day of hardship (ḍank), I alight."

It is applied to the singular, the plural, and the feminine. A group read "ḍankā," making the word "maʿīshah" (life) take the attribute in its feminine form. People differed concerning the straitened life: when is the time in which it occurs? One group said: it is in this world. Their meaning is that the disbeliever, even if his situation and wealth are expansive, still has with him greed, hope, and torment through worldly matters and desire, and the expansion of the clarity of life through these things becomes for him a straitened life. Another group said: it is straitened through eating what is unlawful. Another group said: rather, the straitened life is in the barzakh (intermediate state), namely that he sees his seat in the Fire morning and evening. In sum, it is the punishment of the grave, according to what has been related concerning it.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The interpretation of this group is that the wording of the verse requires that the straitened life be before the Day of Resurrection, by His saying, "and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind," and by His saying, exalted is He, "But the punishment of the Hereafter is harsher and more lasting" [Ṭā-Hā: 127]. Another group said: rather, the straitened life is in the Hereafter, and it is their punishment in Jahannam and their eating of al-zaqqūm and other things. God, exalted is He, mentioned that as a threat against them. Then He informed about another state, which is also on the Day of Resurrection, namely their being gathered blind. Then His saying, "But the punishment of the Hereafter is harsher and more lasting" [Ṭā-Hā: 127] comes. The meaning of what we have mentioned of the straitened life, blindness, and the like is that it is His punishment in the Hereafter, and it is harsher and more lasting than anything that can be imagined or conceived. It is as if He mentioned a type of the punishment of the Hereafter, and then mentioned that the punishment of the Hereafter is harsher and more lasting.

A group read "wa-naḥshuruhu" with the nūn, and a group read "wa-yaḥshuruhu" (with the yāʾ), and a group read "wa-naḥshuruhu" with the rāʾ sukūn (sukūn on the rāʾ). A group read "aʿmā" with a fatḥah on the alif, and a group read "aʿmā" with imālah. A group said: blindness here is blindness of insight regarding the proof.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Had this been the meaning, the disbeliever would not perceive that, since he died blind of insight and will be gathered in that state. Another group said: blindness is blindness of sight.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is the more apparent view, although blindness of insight is present in both interpretations. As for His saying, exalted is He, "And We will gather the criminals on that Day blue-eyed" [Ṭā-Hā: 102], whoever understands it as "in the eye" must necessarily interpret it along with this, either by saying that it refers to two groups or to two places.

His saying, exalted is He, "Thus Our signs came to you" — "dhālika" (thus) is a reference to the blindness that befell him, i.e., the like of this in the world: that Our signs came to you, and you forgot them. "Al-nisyān" (forgetting) in this verse means abandonment, and there is no place for heedlessness in this context. "Tunsā" means: you will be abandoned in the punishment. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning a man of the Quraysh.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 127–130:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And thus We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the signs of their Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.﴾ ﴿Has it not guided them how many generations We destroyed before them, through whose dwellings they walk? Indeed, in that are signs for people of intellect.﴾ ﴿And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term.﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and exalt your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night exalt Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased.﴾

The meaning: Just as We have described the painful deeds, We recompense those who exceed the limits, the disbelievers in Allah, the Exalted and Majestic. As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾: if the "narrow life" (ma'ishat al-dank) is in this world or in the barzakh (the intermediate state), then this is a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter after a warning. If the "narrow life" is in the Hereafter, then this statement emphasises the warning itself, by which the punishment of the Hereafter is placed above every punishment that a human can imagine or that occurs in this world.

Then He began to rebuke them and remind them of lessons, with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ One group recited *yahdi* with a *ya'* (يَهْدِ), meaning "become clear" (yatabayyan). This group differed about the subject (fa'il) of the verb. Some of them said the subject is *kam* (كَمْ, "how many"). This is a Kufan view, but the grammarians of Basra do not permit it, because *kam* has the front position in the sentence. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "Has it not guided them whom We destroyed?" It seems that this recitation fits that interpretation of *kam*. Others said the subject is Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and the meaning is: Has it not guided them to what Allah has placed for them of signs and lessons? By this way the verb is attributed to Allah, the Exalted; this was said by al-Zajjaj. Others said the subject is implied: guidance, or the matter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Or it is reflection and consideration. This is the best that can be assumed in my view.

One group recited *nahdi* with a *nun* (نَهْدِ), and this recitation fits the interpretation of those who said, regarding the previous one, that the subject is Allah. According to these views, *kam* is in the accusative governed by *ahlaknā* ("We destroyed"). Then He restricted "the generations" by saying that these disbelievers walk through their dwellings. He meant 'Ad, Thamud, and the peoples whose lands Quraysh passed through on their journeys to Syria and elsewhere. One group recited *yamshūna* ("they walk") with a *fatha* on the *ya'*, and one group recited *yumashshawna* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, a *fatha* on the *mim*, and a shadda on the *shin*. *Al-nuhā* is the plural of *nuhya*, which is that which restrains a person from doing what is ugly.

Then the Exalted and Majestic informed that the punishment would have become inevitable for them, were it not for a word that had preceded from Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, regarding delaying it from them until a specified term with Him. So the sense of the sentence is: "Were it not for a word that preceded regarding the delay until a specified term, the punishment would have been inevitable," just as you say: "it would have been decisive or necessarily occurring." But the order has been rearranged so that the ends of the verses rhyme.

People differed about the term (ajal). It may mean the Day of Resurrection, and the punishment threatened according to this is the punishment of Hell. It may also mean by the term the death of each one of them, and the punishment according to this is what they meet in their graves and after. It may also mean by the term the Day of Badr, and the punishment according to this is their being killed by the sword. A group said according to each of the possibilities we have mentioned, and in Sahih al-Bukhari it is stated that the Day of Badr is the *lizam* (inevitable punishment), and it is the great seizing.

Then He, blessed and exalted, commanded him to be patient over their sayings: that he is a magician, that he is a soothsayer, that he is a liar, and other such things. The meaning: do not concern yourself with them, for they are approaching destruction. The fact that the *lizam* was on the Day of Badr is more eloquent as a sign of our Prophet (ﷺ).

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And exalt your Lord with praise﴾. Most of the interpreters said this is a reference to the five prayers. ﴿Before the rising of the sun﴾: the Fajr prayer. ﴿And before its setting﴾: the 'Asr prayer. ﴿And during the hours of the night﴾: the 'Isha' prayer. ﴿And at the ends of the day﴾: the Maghrib and the Zuhr. Another group said: ﴿during the hours of the night﴾ refers to Maghrib and 'Isha', and "the ends of the day" refers only to Zuhr. The wording may also mean the saying "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him" after the Fajr prayer until the two rak'as of Duha, and before the sun sets. For the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever glorifies Allah at the setting of the sun with one glorification, his sins will set with it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He called the two extremes "ends" (atraf) in one of two ways: either in the manner of His saying, ﴿Your hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], or by making *al-nahar* (the day) a generic noun, so that each day has an end, and these are the ones he gathered. As for the one who said "the ends of the day" refers to the Zuhr prayer alone, he must rely on the day being generic, as we said, or say that the day divides into two parts separated by the zawal (the sun's decline at midday), and each part has two ends. So at the zawal there are two ends: the last of the first part and the first of the second part. Thus He said "ends" regarding the two extremes, in the manner of ﴿Your hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. Abu Bakr ibn Furak alluded to this line of thought in *al-Mushkil*.

*Al-anha'* is the plural of *ina*, which is an hour of the night. From it is the saying of the Hudhali poet:

*Sweet and bitter, like the turning of an arrow-shaft, it struck him at every hour; the judges of the night put on their sandals.*

Some said: the verse refers to supererogatory prayers. Among them are the hours of the night, and among them the time before sunrise, and the two rak'as of Fajr and Maghrib are the ends of the day. Al-Jumhur (the majority) recited *la'allaka tarda* ("that you may be pleased") with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, meaning: that you may be rewarded for these deeds with what pleases you. Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, recited *la'allaka turda* with a *damma* on the *ta'*, meaning: that you may be given what gratifies you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 131–133:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them thereby. The provision of your Lord is better and more lasting.﴾ ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the good outcome is for righteousness.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾

Some people have said: the cause of this verse is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a guest come to him, and he had nothing. So he sent to a Jew to borrow barley, but the Jew refused except against a pledge. The Messenger informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of this, and he said: "By Allah, I am trustworthy in the heavens and trustworthy on the earth." So he pledged his coat of mail to him, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is objectionable as a cause, because the surah is Meccan, while the incident mentioned is Medinan, at the very end of the Prophet's life (ﷺ), since he died while his coat of mail was pledged over this very incident that was mentioned. Rather, the apparent meaning is that the verse coheres with what precedes it, for Allah the Exalted rebuked them for failing to take warning from earlier nations, then threatened them with a deferred punishment, then commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to disregard their affairs, to endure their words, and to turn away from their wealth and what they hold of worldly things, since that is cut off from them and leads them only to disgrace.

(p-147) His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And do not strain your eyes﴾ is more emphatic than "and do not look," because one who strains his gaze is driven to it by an attached covetousness, whereas one who merely looks may not have that with him. And "al-azwaj" means the kinds, so it is as if He said: "to what We have given enjoyment to groups of them and categories." His saying ﴿the splendour of the life of this world﴾ likens the blessings of these disbelievers to blossoms (zahr), which is what has turned yellow of light. It is also said that zahr is light in general, because a blossom has an appearance and then fades, and so is the state of these people. The accusative of "zahrata" may be by supposing a verb, its estimate being "We made it a blossom," or it may be in the state (ḥāl) position, since its definiteness is not pure. One group read "zahratan" with tanwin, another read "zahrata" with the ha' sukūn, and another "zahara" with fatḥa on the ha'. And the provision of Allah the Exalted, which He made lawful for the God-fearing among His servants, is better and more lasting; that is, the provision of this world is good, and the provision of the Hereafter is more lasting, and He clarified that it is better than the provision of this world.

Then He, blessed and exalted, commanded him to command his family to pray, and to join them in it, and to persevere in it and remain constant in it, and He undertook his provision Himself, there is no god but Him, and informed him that the good outcome is for the people of God-consciousness and within its domain; for there is the victory of Allah in this world and His mercy in the Hereafter. It is narrated that 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him), whenever he saw something of the reports of rulers and their conditions, would hasten to his home, enter it while reciting this verse, ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them thereby. The majority read "naḥnu narzuquka" with a ḍamma on the qaf, and one group read "naḥnu narzuqka" with sukūn on it.

His saying ﴿the splendour of the life of this world﴾ likens the blessings of these disbelievers to blossoms (zahr), which is what has turned yellow of light. It is also said that zahr is light in general, because a blossom has an appearance and then fades, and so is the state of these people. The accusative of "zahrata" may be by supposing a verb, its estimate being "We made it a blossom," or it may be in the state (ḥāl) position, since its definiteness is not pure. One group read "zahratan" with tanwin, another read "zahrata" with the ha' sukūn, and another "zahara" with fatḥa on the ha'. Then Allah the Exalted informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that this is only so that He may test them by it, and make it a trial for them and a matter for which they are repaid with evil because of their corrupt fluctuation in it. And the provision of Allah the Exalted, which He made lawful for the God-fearing among His servants, is better and more lasting; that is, the provision of this world is good, and the provision of the Hereafter is more lasting, and He clarified that it is better than the provision of this world.

Then He, blessed and exalted, commanded him to command his family to pray, and to join them in it, and to persevere in it and remain constant in it, and He undertook his provision Himself, there is no god but Him, and informed him that the good outcome is for the people of God-consciousness and within its domain; for there is the victory of Allah in this world and His mercy in the Hereafter. This address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and all his community enters within its generality. It is narrated that 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him), whenever he saw something of the reports of rulers and their conditions, would hasten to his home, enter it while reciting this verse, ﴿And do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world, that We may test them thereby. The provision of your Lord is better and more lasting.﴾ Then he would call out: "The prayer, the prayer; may Allah have mercy on you," and pray. And the Commander of the Faithful 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) (p-148) would wake the people of his household for the night prayer, pray, and invoke this verse as an admonition. The majority read "naḥnu narzuquka" with a ḍamma on the qaf, and one group read "naḥnu narzuqka" with sukūn on it.

Then Allah the Exalted related concerning groups of the disbelievers who said about Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?﴾ That is, a sign from what we have proposed to him, or something that overwhelms and compels.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The messengers of Allah were only accompanied by signs presented for consideration, enveloped by rational proofs, so that whoever Allah's knowledge had already decreed to be misguided would go astray, and whoever was already decreed guidance would be guided. Thus Allah the Exalted rebuked them with His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ meaning the Torah, the greatest witness and the greatest sign for it. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read "ta'tihim" in agreement with the word "bayyina," while the rest, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, read "ya'tihim" with the ya' in consideration of the meaning. One group read "bayyinatu ma fi al-suhuf" with idafa to "ma," and one group read "bayyinatun" with tanwin, with "ma" then being an apposition (badal) in this reading; and one group read "bayyinata ma" with the accusative, and "ma" in this reading is the subject (fa'il) of "ta'ti." The majority read "fi al-suhuf" with a ḍamma on the ḥa', and one group read "fi al-suhf" with sukūn on it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 20, verses 134–135:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Each is waiting, so wait. You will soon know who are the companions of the even path (al-sirat al-sawi) and who has been guided."﴾

Allah informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that if He had destroyed this disbelieving nation before sending Muhammad (ﷺ) to them, a proof would have been established against them, and they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger..." to the end of the verse. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Three will argue before Allah on the Day of Resurrection: the one who died in the interval (al-fatra) between prophets, the one who was mentally incapacitated, and the young child. The mentally incapacitated person will say: 'My Lord, why did You not give me intellect?' The child will say the same. The one who died in the interval will say: 'O Lord, why did You not send a messenger to me? Had he come to me, I would have been the most obedient of Your creatures to You.' He said: Then a fire will be raised before them, and it will be said to them: 'Enter it.' He said: Whoever was known in Allah's knowledge to be among the blessed will enter it, and the wretched one will hold back from it. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, will say: 'It was Me that you disobeyed, so how much more would you have disobeyed My messengers had they come to you?'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

As for the child and the mentally incapacitated person, their situation is clear. As for the person of the interval, he is not like the disbelievers of Quraysh before the Prophet (ﷺ), because the disbelievers of Quraysh and others who knew and heard of prophethood and messagehood in the regions of the earth are not people of the interval. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the man who asked him about his father: "My father and your father are in the Fire," and he saw 'Amr ibn Luhayy in the Fire, along with other matters too long to mention. The person of the interval is one who is assumed to be a human being to whom it never reached that Allah the Exalted had sent a messenger or called to a religion. This is rarely found, except that it may occur in remote corners of the earth cut off from civilization. Humiliation and disgrace accompany the punishment of the Hereafter.

Then Allah commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to threaten them and to urge them and himself to patient waiting (al-tarabbus) and expectation of relief. "Al-tarabbus" means to wait patiently, and "al-sirat" means the path. One group read: "min ashab al-sirat al-sawi," and another group read: "al-sirat al-sawa'," as if this verse divided the two groups, i.e., you will know this from that. Another group read: "al-sirat al-sawwa" with a doubled and fatha-vowelled waw, and another group read: "al-sirat al-suwa" with a damma on the sin and a hamza upon the waw, on the pattern of fa'la. "Man ihtada" means: was rightly guided.

The commentary on Surah Ta-Ha is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
